subject: Test 12 — Modern History II (1885 to 1947 & onwards)

questions.q: The Unionist Party emerged as a major political force in which of the following provinces during the provincial elections of 1937?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Unionist Party, formally known as the Punjab National Unionist Party, emerged as the dominant political force in Punjab and formed the government following the provincial elections of 1937. The party had been founded in 1923 by Sir Fazl-i-Husain, with the active collaboration of Chaudhary Chhotu Ram representing Hindu Jat interests and Sir Sikandar Hayat Khan representing Muslim landed interests. Its ideological foundation was distinctive and deliberate; rather than organising along religious lines as most other political formations of the era did, the Unionist Party built its support base around agrarian and landed interests, cutting across the religious divide of Muslims, Hindus, and Sikhs who shared common economic interests as rural proprietors and zamindars of Punjab.

In the 1937 elections, the Unionist Party won a decisive majority in the Punjab Legislative Assembly, and Sir Sikandar Hayat Khan, who had become the party’s leader following Fazl-i-Husain’s declining health, formed the government. The party’s success demonstrated that in Punjab’s particular socioeconomic context, class and agrarian identity could override religious identity as the primary basis of political mobilisation. The Unionist government maintained its cross-communal character through a coalition arrangement, the Sikandar-Jinnah Pact of 1937, whereby Punjab Muslim League members in the assembly agreed to support the Unionist government, though the Unionist Party itself retained its distinct identity separate from the All India Muslim League.

questions.q: Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order: 1. Formation of the National Planning Committee 2. Provincial Elections under the Government of India Act, 1935 3. Resignation of the Congress Ministries 4. Wardha Scheme of Basic Education Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.question_type: Chronological Order — Correct Sequence
questions.explanation:
The correct chronological sequence places the Provincial Elections first, followed by the Wardha Scheme, then the National Planning Committee, and finally the Resignation of Congress Ministries.

The Provincial Elections under the Government of India Act, 1935, were held in February 1937, marking the first major exercise of provincial self-governance under the new constitutional framework. Congress contested these elections and won decisive majorities in several provinces, eventually forming ministries in July 1937 after resolving its initial deadlock with the British over the governors’ special powers.

The Wardha Scheme of Basic Education was followed in October 1937, when Gandhi convened the All India National Education Conference at Wardha. The Zakir Hussain Committee was subsequently formed to work out the detailed curriculum, and the scheme was formally articulated as a comprehensive craft-centred educational philosophy over the following months.

The National Planning Committee was formed in 1938, under the chairmanship of Jawaharlal Nehru, by the Indian National Congress at its Haripura Session presided over by Subhas Chandra Bose. It was constituted to develop a blueprint for India’s economic development and industrialisation, bringing together experts, scientists, industrialists, and Congress leaders to deliberate on planned economic development for independent India.

The Resignation of the Congress Ministries occurred in October-November 1939, following Viceroy Linlithgow’s unilateral declaration of India’s participation in World War II without consulting elected Indian representatives, which prompted the Congress Working Committee to direct all its provincial ministries to resign.

questions.q: The Pirpur Report and Shareef Report were associated with:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.C: Inquiry into communal riots in Punjab

questions.explanation:
The Pirpur Report and the Shareef Report were both documents produced by the All India Muslim League to catalogue alleged grievances and complaints of Muslims living under Congress provincial ministries during 1937-39.

The Pirpur Report, formally titled the Report of the Enquiry Committee of the All India Muslim League, was prepared in 1938 under the chairmanship of Raja Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur. It compiled a detailed list of allegations against Congress ministries in various provinces, claiming that Muslims were subjected to cultural suppression, economic discrimination, and political marginalisation under Congress rule. Specific grievances included the imposition of the Bande Mataram song, which the League argued contained Hindu religious symbolism unacceptable to Muslims, the promotion of Hindi in the Devanagari script over Urdu, the Vidya Mandir scheme of education in the Central Provinces, which allegedly had a Hindu cultural orientation, and various instances of alleged bias in government appointments and administration.

The Shareef Report, formally known as the Report on the Condition of Muslims under Congress Ministries, was submitted in 1939 by a committee headed by A. K. Shareef and focused specifically on Bihar, further elaborating the Muslim League’s charge that Congress ministries were systematically neglecting or suppressing Muslim interests.

Both reports served a significant political purpose for Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League; they were used to mobilise Muslim public opinion against the Congress, to counter the Congress’s claim of being a genuinely representative all-India national organisation, and to build the narrative that Muslims could not expect fair treatment under Congress-dominated governance. Historians have debated the factual accuracy and political motivations of these reports extensively. Many Congress leaders and secular historians argued they were largely exaggerated or politically motivated documents rather than objective inquiries, but their political impact in sharpening the Congress-League divide during the critical years leading up to the Lahore Resolution of 1940 was undeniable.

questions.q: Which of the following events took place at the Haripura Session of the Indian National Congress (1938)?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Subhas Chandra Bose was elected after defeating Pattabhi Sitaramayya
options.B: Subhas Chandra Bose was elected unopposed as Congress President
options.C: Congress adopted the Quit India Resolution
options.D: Jawaharlal Nehru was appointed chairman of the Planning Commission

questions.explanation: At the Haripura Session of 1938, held in Gujarat, Subhas Chandra Bose was elected Congress President unopposed, a significant distinction from his controversial re-election the following year. The Haripura Session was notable for its grand organisation, supervised by Vallabhbhai Patel, and for the National Planning Committee being constituted under Nehru’s chairmanship on Bose’s initiative.

questions.q: Which of the following conditions was laid down by the Congress Working Committee in its Wardha Resolution (1939) for extending support to the British war effort?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.C: Transfer of power to princely states

questions.explanation:
The Wardha Resolution of September 1939, passed by the Congress Working Committee in response to Viceroy Linlithgow’s unilateral declaration of India’s participation in World War II, laid down that Congress could not support a war effort conducted under imperial auspices unless Britain made a clear and concrete commitment to Indian independence.

The resolution demanded that Britain explicitly declare that the war was being fought for democracy and self-determination, and that these principles be applied to India without ambiguity or delay.

Congress insisted on knowing whether India would be free to frame its own constitution after the war, and sought a definitive statement of British war aims with respect to imperialism and colonial rule. When Linlithgow’s October 1939 response offered only vague post-war consultations rather than any firm commitment, Congress directed its ministries to resign.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the August Offer (1940): 1. Dominion Status was declared as the objective of British policy in India. 2. Expansion of the Viceroy’s Executive Council was proposed. 3. Minorities were assured that no constitutional arrangement would be imposed without their consent. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The August Offer explicitly reaffirmed Dominion Status as the objective for India after the conclusion of the war, along with a promise that Indians would be primarily responsible for framing the new constitutional arrangement through a post-war constituent body. However, by this stage, Congress had moved well beyond Dominion Status and was demanding complete independence, making the offer unacceptable.

Statement 2 is correct: The offer proposed the immediate expansion of the Viceroy’s Executive Council to include a greater number of Indian representatives as a wartime political concession. However, since the expanded council would continue to function under the Viceroy’s overriding authority, Congress considered this inadequate and rejected it.

Statement 3 is correct: The August Offer assured that the British government would not transfer power to any authority whose exercise would be opposed by large and powerful elements in India’s national life, effectively granting minorities, particularly the Muslim League, a veto over future constitutional arrangements. This significantly strengthened Jinnah’s bargaining position and deepened Congress’s distrust of British intentions. Both Congress and the Muslim League rejected the August Offer, though for entirely different reasons.

questions.q: The Individual Satyagraha launched in 1940 primarily aimed to:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Force immediate British withdrawal from India
options.B: Assert the right to free speech without seriously embarrassing the British war effort
options.C: Launch mass civil disobedience across provinces

questions.explanation:
The Individual Satyagraha, launched by Gandhi in October 1940 after the rejection of the August Offer, was conceived as a limited and carefully controlled movement, not a mass confrontation. Its objective was to affirm the Indian people’s right to freedom of speech and expression, particularly the right to oppose India’s forced participation in World War II without Indian consent.

Gandhi deliberately avoided launching a fullscale mass movement at this stage because the international wartime situation was sensitive, and he did not wish to create a situation that would directly cripple the British war effort at that moment. Hence, selected individuals, beginning with Vinoba Bhave (the first satyagrahi) and later Jawaharlal Nehru, were chosen to publicly make anti-war statements and court arrest.

questions.q: Arrange the following individual satyagrahis associated with the Individual Satyagraha (1940– 41) in the correct sequence of their selection by Mahatma Gandhi: 1. Jawaharlal Nehru 2. Vinoba Bhave 3. Brahma Datt Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.question_type: Ordering/Ranking — Correct Sequence
questions.explanation:
Vinoba Bhave was deliberately chosen by Gandhi as the first individual satyagrahi. This choice was itself politically significant, as Bhave was relatively unknown to the wider public compared to senior Congress leaders. Gandhi selected him to emphasise personal moral conviction, discipline, and selfless commitment over political stature. Bhave delivered his symbolic anti-war speech at Paunar in October 1940 and was promptly arrested, formally inaugurating the movement.

Jawaharlal Nehru was chosen as the second satyagrahi, a decision carrying considerable political weight given his national prominence and international visibility. His arrest following his anti-war statement drew widespread attention within India and abroad, substantially amplifying the movement’s political and moral message.

Brahma Datt, a close associate of Gandhi from the Sevagram Ashram, was selected as the third satyagrahi. His inclusion reflected Gandhi’s pattern of balancing nationally prominent leaders with committed constructive workers, reinforcing the movement’s character as a disciplined moral protest rather than a mass political confrontation.

The deliberate sequential and individual nature of these selections, with each person making a symbolic anti-war declaration and courting arrest before the next was nominated, was central to Gandhi’s strategy of keeping the movement tightly controlled, disciplined, and morally defensible throughout its course.

questions.q: Where did Mahatma Gandhi give the famous “Do or Die” call in the context of the Quit India Movement?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: At the Congress Working Committee meeting at Wardha in July 1942
options.B: At the All India Congress Committee session at Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay, on 8 August 1942
options.C: At the Lahore session of the Indian National Congress in 1929
options.D: At a meeting marking the first anniversary of the Quit India Movement in 1943

questions.explanation:
Mahatma Gandhi delivered the famous “Do or Die” call at the All India Congress Committee session held at Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay, on the night of 8 August 1942, immediately after the AICC passed the Quit India Resolution demanding an immediate end to British rule.

His speech that night was electrifying. Gandhi called upon every Indian to consider themselves already free and to act with that spirit, declaring that this was the most decisive struggle of his political life. Through the phrase “Do or Die,” he conveyed that Indians must either secure freedom through unwavering struggle or lay down their lives in the attempt, but not continue to live under colonial subjugation.

The British response was immediate and decisive. Within hours of the resolution’s passage, in the early hours of 9 August 1942, Gandhi, the entire Congress Working Committee, and virtually all top Congress leaders were arrested before any centrally coordinated movement could formally begin. This leadership vacuum, however, transformed Quit India into a spontaneous and widespread mass uprising across the country.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs related to parallel governments during the Quit India Movement: 1. Ballia : Associated with Chittu Pandey 2. Tamluk : Jatiya Sarkar 3. Satara : Prati Sarkar Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correctly matched: Chittu Pandey led a brief but dramatic parallel government in Ballia, in the United Provinces, in August 1942. He organised local resistance, released political prisoners from jail, and temporarily displaced British administrative authority in the district before the British reimposed control. Ballia earned the nickname “Baghi Ballia” (Rebel Ballia) for this episode.

Pair 2 is correctly matched: The parallel government established at Tamluk (Tamralipta) in the Midnapore district of Bengal was called the Jatiya Sarkar (National Government), formally proclaimed in December 1942. It functioned for nearly two years, organising relief work, running schools, maintaining law and order, and publishing its own journal -- representing one of the most sustained and administratively functional parallel governments of the movement.

Pair 3 is correctly matched: The Satara Prati Sarkar (Parallel Government) in Maharashtra, led primarily by Nana Patil, was the longest-lasting and best-organised parallel administration of the movement, functioning from 1943 to 1945. It ran its own courts, collected revenue, organised village defence, and carried out social reform activities -- serving as a remarkable example of grassroots selfgovernance in defiance of colonial authority.

questions.q: Matangini Hazra is associated with which of the following developments during the Quit India Movement?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.B: The parallel government established at Tamluk
options.C: The Rani Jhansi Regiment of the Indian National Army

questions.explanation: Matangini Hazra, popularly known as “Gandhi Buri” (the old woman Gandhi) for her devoted adherence to Gandhian ideals, is associated with the resistance centred in Tamluk (Tamralipta) in the Midnapore district of Bengal. On 29 September 1942, she led a procession of several thousand people toward the Tamluk police station demanding the release of political prisoners and the withdrawal of British authority. When British police opened fire on the procession, Matangini continued advancing while carrying the Congress flag even after sustaining multiple gunshot wounds, until she fell fatally shot her last words reportedly being “Vande Mataram.” Her martyrdom became a powerful symbol of the resistance in Midnapore, the region that subsequently established the Jatiya Sarkar parallel government in December 1942.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the origins of the Indian National Army (INA): 1. Mohan Singh played a key role in its initial formation. 2. Major Fujiwara assisted in mobilising Indian prisoners of war for the cause. 3. Rash Behari Bose founded the Indian National Army in Berlin. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Captain Mohan Singh, an officer of the British Indian Army captured during the Malayan campaign, played the principal role in the initial formation of the Indian National Army. After the fall of Singapore in February 1942, he began organising Indian prisoners of war into an armed force intended to fight for India’s liberation from British rule. The first INA was formally established in September 1942 under his leadership. However, tensions with the Japanese over questions of autonomy and command led to Mohan Singh’s arrest in December 1942, resulting in the collapse of the first INA.

Statement 2 is correct: Major Iwaichi Fujiwara of Japanese Military Intelligence played a key enabling role in the INA’s early formation. Through the Fujiwara Kikan, a Japanese intelligence unit tasked with cultivating anti-British sentiment among Indian troops, he established contact with Indian POWs and nationalist elements in Malaya. This early groundwork was instrumental in enabling Mohan Singh’s efforts.

Statement 3 is incorrect: Rash Behari Bose did not found the INA in Berlin. He had been living in exile in Japan since 1915 and was the political figure associated with the Indian Independence League in East Asia. He played a major role in the Bangkok Conference (1942), which provided political direction to the INA. The INA emerged in Southeast Asia, particularly Singapore, not Berlin. Subhas Chandra Bose, who reached Southeast Asia in 1943, later assumed leadership and reorganised the INA into a much more effective force under the Azad Hind Government.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Simla Conference (1945): 1. Muhammad Ali Jinnah insisted that the Muslim League alone should nominate all Muslim members to the proposed Executive Council. 2. The Congress claim to represent all communities, including Muslims, became a major point of contention in the negotiations. 3. The conference resulted in the successful formation of an interim national government. How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Jinnah’s insistence that only the Muslim League could nominate Muslim members to the reconstituted Executive Council was the principal reason for the collapse of the Simla Conference. Accepting Muslim nominees from Congress, including nationalist Muslims, would have weakened the League’s claim that it alone represented India’s Muslim community.

Statement 2 is correct: Congress’s position directly conflicted with this claim. Congress maintained that it represented all Indians irrespective of religion and therefore retained the right to nominate members, including Muslims, to the Executive Council. This fundamental clash between Congress’s inclusive nationalist position and the League’s claim of exclusive Muslim representation made compromise impossible.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The Simla Conference ended in failure. Lord Wavell was unable to break the deadlock over the issue of Muslim representation and suspended the conference in July 1945 without any agreement. Consequently, no interim government emerged from the Simla Conference.

questions.q: The Royal Indian Navy Mutiny of 1946 began at which of the following establishments?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The immediate spark for the Royal Indian Navy Mutiny (18 February 1946) occurred at HMIS Talwar, the signal training establishment in Bombay, where around 1,100 Indian ratings went on strike.

The immediate grievances included: • Poor quality food and living conditions • Racial discrimination and abusive treatment by British officers • Deep resentment over broader colonial inequality and the nationalist atmosphere following the INA trials

A particularly direct trigger was the conduct of Commander Arthur Frederick King, whose racially abusive behaviour toward Indian ratings intensified tensions. The strike quickly spread in Bombay itself, with ratings from HMIS Sutlej, HMIS Jumna, Castle Barracks, and Fort Barracks joining in solidarity.

HMIS Hindustan was not part of the initial spark, as it was stationed in Karachi and joined the uprising later as the mutiny spread geographically.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Champaran Satyagraha: 1. The Champaran Agrarian Committee recommended the abolition of the Tinkathia system. 2. The committee recommended a full refund of all illegal dues collected from peasants. 3. Many educated middle-class leaders, such as Rajendra Prasad and J.B. Kripalani, assisted Gandhi during the movement. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Champaran Agrarian Committee, of which Gandhi was a member, recommended the abolition of the exploitative Tinkathia system imposed on indigo cultivators.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The committee did not recommend a complete refund of illegal recoveries. It recommended a refund of 25% of the illegal dues collected from the peasants.

Statement 3 is correct: Several educated middleclass leaders such as Rajendra Prasad, Gorakh Prasad and J. B. Kripalani actively supported Gandhi during the Champaran movement and worked as his close associates.

questions.q: Consider the following reasons: 1. A separate Pakistan would face serious economic and administrative difficulties. 2. Provinces such as Punjab and Bengal had substantial non-Muslim populations, making partition problematic. 3. The British Parliament was opposed in principle to the partition of India. Which of the above reasons were cited by the Cabinet Mission for rejecting the demand for a sovereign Pakistan?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Cabinet Mission rejected the demand for a fully sovereign Pakistan partly on grounds of economic and administrative impracticability. It argued that partition would create serious difficulties relating to defence, communications, financial arrangements, and administrative continuity, particularly because the integrated institutional structure of British India could not be divided without substantial disruption. A truncated Pakistan, especially one deprived of economically interdependent regions, was viewed as structurally weak.

Statement 2 is correct: The Mission also emphasised the demographic complexity of Punjab and Bengal, the two provinces central to the Pakistan demand. Both contained substantial nonMuslim populations, making any neat territorial division along communal lines extremely difficult. Partition of these provinces would itself require further partition, thereby reproducing the minority problem rather than resolving it. This formed a central element of the Mission’s rejection of the Pakistan proposal.

Statement 3 is incorrect: Opposition from the British Parliament was not cited as a formal reason for rejecting Pakistan. The Cabinet Mission’s objections were framed in practical constitutional terms, focusing on administrative feasibility, economic viability, defence considerations, and demographic realities rather than parliamentary reluctance.

questions.q: Which of the statements regarding the Direct Action Day is incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct

options.A: It was called by Muhammad Ali Jinnah after the breakdown of the Cabinet Mission framework.
options.B: It led to the communal violence known as the Great Calcutta Killings.
options.C: H.S. Suhrawardy was associated with the events that unfolded in Bengal.
options.D: It was formally supported by the Unionist Party government in Punjab as part of a coordinated all-India political mobilisation.

questions.explanation:
Statement A is correct: Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) was called by the Muslim League after its withdrawal from the Cabinet Mission framework, primarily due to the dispute over the compulsory nature of provincial grouping and the broader constitutional deadlock with Congress. It marked the League’s shift from constitutional negotiation to mass political mobilisation in pursuit of Pakistan.

Statement B is correct: Direct Action Day precipitated the Great Calcutta Killings, one of the most severe episodes of communal violence in late colonial India. The violence lasted several days and caused thousands of deaths, after which communal disturbances spread to Noakhali and Bihar, intensifying communal polarisation and significantly strengthening the political momentum toward partition.

Statement C is correct: H. S. Suhrawardy, the Muslim League Chief Minister of Bengal, remains controversially associated with the Calcutta violence. His administration has been criticised for administrative inaction and inadequate preventive measures, though the extent of direct political complicity remains a matter of historical debate.

Statement D is incorrect: The Unionist Party in Punjab, led by Malik Khizar Hayat Tiwana, was not aligned with the Muslim League’s all-India mobilisation strategy. On the contrary, Khizar’s ministry resisted League pressure, and the political confrontation between the two intensified until his resignation in 1947.

questions.q: Attlee’s Declaration of 20 February 1947 announced which of the following?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Immediate grant of independence to India
options.B: Acceptance of the compulsory grouping scheme under the Cabinet Mission Plan
options.C: Immediate creation of Pakistan as a separate dominion
options.D: Transfer of power to responsible Indian hands by June 30, 1948

questions.explanation:
Attlee’s Declaration of 20 February 1947 announced that Britain would transfer power to “responsible Indian hands” no later than June 1948, establishing for the first time a definitive public deadline for British withdrawal from India. The declaration also announced the replacement of Lord Wavell by Lord Mountbatten as Viceroy, signalling a new political approach toward concluding the transfer of power. The significance of the declaration lay in its essentially unconditional character, Britain committed itself to withdrawal by the stated deadline irrespective of whether Indian political parties had reached a constitutional settlement. This transformed the negotiating environment by making indefinite delay politically impossible and placing immediate pressure on both the Congress and the Muslim League to resolve the constitutional deadlock.

Mountbatten subsequently compressed the timetable further, advancing the transfer of power from the announced June 1948 deadline to August 1947.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the integration of Hyderabad into the Indian Union: 1. The Nizam of Hyderabad resisted accession to India. 2. The Razakars actively supported the Hyderabad regime against integration. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Nizam Mir Osman Ali Khan resisted accession to India after independence, seeking either full independence or a special treaty relationship that would preserve Hyderabad’s autonomous status. He signed only a Standstill Agreement with India in November 1947 to temporarily maintain existing administrative arrangements, while also exploring international avenues, including approaches concerning external recognition. From India’s perspective, Hyderabad’s claim to independence was strategically unacceptable given its location as a landlocked state entirely surrounded by Indian territory.

Statement 2 is correct: The Razakars, the paramilitary wing associated with the Majlis-eIttehadul Muslimeen under Qasim Razvi, actively supported the Nizam’s refusal to integrate with India. Their violent activities, including intimidation of the Hindu population and incursions affecting neighbouring Indian areas, significantly worsened the situation. Their actions reinforced Sardar Patel’s conclusion that negotiations had failed and that military intervention had become necessary, culminating in Operation Polo in September 1948.

questions.q: Which of the following leaders were associated with the Champaran Satyagraha? 1. Rajendra Prasad 2. J.B. Kripalani 3. Anugrah Narayan Sinha 4. Bipin Chandra Pal Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Rajendra Prasad was one of the prominent leaders who assisted Mahatma Gandhi during the Champaran Satyagraha.

Statement 2 is correct: J. B. Kripalani actively participated in the Champaran movement and worked closely with Gandhi during the enquiry into peasant grievances.

Statement 3 is correct: Anugrah Narayan Sinha was among the important local leaders associated with the Champaran Satyagraha.

Statement 4 is incorrect: Bipin Chandra Pal was a prominent extremist nationalist leader, but he was not directly associated with the Champaran Satyagraha.

questions.q: Mountbatten referred to Mahatma Gandhi by which of the following descriptions?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Lord Mountbatten gave Gandhi the title ‘One-Man Boundary Force’ during the 1947 Partition riots. He observed that while a 50,000-strong military boundary force completely failed to stop the massive communal violence in Punjab, Gandhi’s solitary presence, moral authority, and fasting in Bengal (specifically in Calcutta and Noakhali) successfully brought the rioting there to a halt. Mountbatten famously marvelled that what an entire army couldn’t achieve in the West, one man achieved in the East.

questions.q: In which year was the Communist Party of India formally established in India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Communist Party of India was formally founded within India during the Kanpur Communist Conference in December 1925.

Additional facts: • The initial formation of the Communist Party of India took place in Tashkent in October 1920. • Founding members of the Tashkent group included M. N. Roy, Evelyn Roy, Abani Mukherji, Rosa Fitingof, Mohammad Ali, and Mohammad Shafiq. • M. N. Roy was the first Indian elected to the leadership of the Communist International (Comintern). • In 1924, the British government arrested S. A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmad, Shaukat Usmani, and Nalini Gupta in the Kanpur Bolshevik Conspiracy Case. • The 1925 Kanpur Communist Conference was primarily organised by Satyabhakta. • S. V. Ghate became the first Secretary of the CPI after the 1925 Kanpur Conference. • In the late 1920s, communists operated openly through various provincial Workers’ and Peasants’ Parties. • The government launched a massive crackdown on communist leadership in March 1929 through the Meerut Conspiracy Case.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the All India Kisan Sabha: 1. Swami Sahajanand Saraswati presided over the inaugural session of the All India Kisan Sabha. 2. Indulal Yagnik was officially appointed as the General Secretary during this first conference. 3. It finalised and adopted a Kisan Manifesto in 1936. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati, the founder of the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha, was elected as the first President.

Statement 2 is incorrect: N. G. Ranga, a prominent agrarian leader from Andhra, was elected as the General Secretary; Indulal Yagnik was instead tasked with managing the organisation’s publications.

Statement 3 is correct: The All India Kisan Committee officially finalised and adopted the comprehensive Kisan Manifesto during its subsequent meeting in Bombay in August 1936.

Additional facts: • The inaugural session of the All India Kisan Sabha took place in Lucknow during April 1936. • This foundational conference deliberately coincided with the annual session of the Indian National Congress being held in the same city. • Jawaharlal Nehru personally attended the first All India Kisan Sabha conference and delivered an address to the gathered peasant leaders. • Indulal Yagnik officially launched and edited the organisation’s primary periodical, which was titled the Kisan Bulletin. • The finalised Kisan Manifesto heavily influenced the official agrarian reform program adopted by the Indian National Congress at its Faizpur session. • The Faizpur Congress session was the first to feature a concurrent, massive All India Kisan Conference right next to the main pavilion. • A core objective of the Sabha was the complete abolition of the zamindari and taluqdari systems of land revenue. • The organisation actively demanded the immediate reduction of land revenue and rent by at least fifty percent. • The Sabha organised nationwide mass agitations demanding the formal abolition of begar (forced, unpaid agricultural labour). • Prominent regional peasant organisers like Karyanand Sharma, Yadunandan Sharma, and Rahul Sankrityayan heavily integrated their local movements into this new all-India framework.

questions.q: Whose assassination by a local landlord’s thugs immediately sparked the militant phase of the Telangana struggle?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The targeted murder of Doddi Komarayya, a local village militant, by the armed retainers of the Visnur Deshmukh in July 1946 served as the immediate catalyst for the mass armed uprising.

Makhdoom Mohiuddin, P. Sundarayya, and Ravi Narayan Reddy were prominent Communist leaders who strategically directed this movement.

Additional facts: • The Telangana Rebellion (Telangana Movement) occurred from 1946 to 1951, making it the biggest peasant guerrilla war in modern Indian history. • Vetti System: Landlords (deshmukhs and jagirdars) routinely extracted an institutionalised form of unpaid, forced agricultural labour known locally as vetti. • Andhra Mahasabha Platform: The Communist Party of India mobilised rural masses using the regional platform of the Andhra Mahasabha. • Dalams (Armed Guerrilla Squads): Peasant activists organised mobile, armed guerrilla squads functioning under the designation dalams. • Gram Rajyams (Village Soviets): Revolutionary cadres successfully established parallel administrative structures called gram rajyams (village soviets) across approximately 3,000 villages. • Land Redistribution: The movement successfully confiscated and redistributed nearly 1 million acres of agricultural land to landless labourers and tenants. • Razakar Conflict: Guerrilla forces engaged in sustained armed combat against the Nizam’s private Islamic paramilitary organisation, the Razakars, commanded by Qasim Razvi. • Post-Operation Polo Resistance: The rural insurgency maintained its armed posture against the state even after the Indian Army annexed Hyderabad via Operation Polo (September 1948). • CPI Suspension: The Communist Party leadership formally suspended the armed agrarian campaign in October 1951 to participate in the upcoming general elections. • Doddi Komarayya’s Background: He belonged to the Kuruma (Shepherd) caste from Kadivendi village of Jangaon taluq and was the first among 4,000 communist and peasant revolutionaries killed in the Telangana People’s Revolutionary Movement. • Statue in Moscow: A statue of Doddi Komaraiah was built in Moscow by the Russians, recognising his significance in the international communist movement. • Casualties: Approximately 4,000 communist and peasant revolutionaries were killed by the ruling classes, represented by the Nizam of Hyderabad. • The Communist Party leadership formally suspended the armed agrarian campaign in October 1951 to participate in the upcoming general elections.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Ahmedabad Mill Workers’ Strike of 1918: 1. The dispute arose over the withdrawal of the plague bonus given to workers. 2. Mahatma Gandhi demanded a 50 per cent wage increase for the workers. 3. Gandhi undertook his first fast unto death during the movement. 4. The tribunal ultimately awarded the workers a 35 per cent wage hike. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Ahmedabad Mill Workers’ Strike began in 1918 after mill owners decided to withdraw the plague bonus that had earlier been granted to workers.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Gandhi advised the workers to demand a 35 per cent increase in wages instead of the originally demanded 50 per cent hike.

Statement 3 is correct: During the strike, Gandhi undertook his first fast unto death to strengthen the determination of the workers and pressure the mill owners for a settlement.

Statement 4 is correct: The dispute was eventually referred to a tribunal, which awarded the workers a 35 per cent wage increase.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the All India States’ Peoples’ Conference: 1. Jawaharlal Nehru was formally elected as the President during the 1939 Ludhiana session. 2. The Haripura Congress session officially initiated direct institutional intervention in princely state agitations. Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Jawaharlal Nehru was elected as the President at the historic Ludhiana session in 1939, signifying the mainstreaming of the states’ struggles.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The Haripura session (1938) explicitly maintained a policy of nonintervention by the institutional Congress; it was the subsequent Tripuri session (1939) that formally endorsed direct organisational intervention in the political agitations of the princely states.

Additional facts: • The All India States’ Peoples’ Conference was originally founded in December 1927 in Bombay to politically unify fragmented regional movements. • Balwantrai Mehta, Maniklal Kothari, and G. R. Abhyankar served as the primary architects who organised the inaugural 1927 conference. • The 1938 Haripura Congress resolution explicitly prohibited local Congress committees from initiating direct political movements inside princely territories. • Under these Haripura guidelines, activists in princely states were strictly mandated to operate through independent, localised political organisations known as Praja Mandals. • Unprecedented mass political awakenings in states like Rajkot, Jaipur, and Travancore forced the Congress leadership to abandon this non-interventionist doctrine. • Following the 1939 Tripuri resolution, these regional Praja Mandals were gradually integrated as active, subordinate units of the overarching Conference. • The organisation consistently campaigned for the immediate establishment of responsible democratic governance under the constitutional aegis of the respective ruling princes. • The British colonial administration legally classified princely states as distinct sovereign entities operating completely outside the constitutional jurisdiction of British India. • Jawaharlal Nehru actively emphasised that the political fate of the princely states was structurally and legally inseparable from the broader Indian independence struggle. • The organisation fiercely opposed the federal provisions of the Government of India Act 1935, which allowed princes to nominate unaccountable representatives to the federal legislature.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Anti-Compromise Conference of 1940: 1. It was held at Ramgarh under the presidentship of Subhas Chandra Bose. 2. Swami Sahajananda Saraswati participated actively in it. 3. It endorsed compromise with British imperial authorities as a temporary strategy. Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Anti-Compromise Conference of 1940 was held at Ramgarh, in present-day Jharkhand, in March 1940, significantly, at the same venue where the official Indian National Congress session was being held under the presidentship of Maulana Abul Kalam Azad. Subhas Chandra Bose, who had by then resigned from the Congress presidency following the fallout of the Tripuri Session and founded the Forward Bloc in 1939, organised and presided over this parallel conference as a platform to voice uncompromising opposition to British imperialism and to challenge the moderate tendencies within the mainstream nationalist movement.

Statement 2 is correct: Swami Sahajananda Saraswati, the prominent kisan leader and founder of the All India Kisan Sabha, actively participated in the Anti-Compromise Conference. His involvement reflected the broader coalition of leftleaning, radical, and agrarian forces that Bose sought to bring together under a united anti-imperialist platform. Sahajananda’s participation underscored the conference’s character as a gathering of those who firmly rejected any accommodation with British colonial authority during the freedom struggle.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The Anti-Compromise Conference was convened to oppose and reject any compromise with British imperial authorities. The conference demanded an immediate and unconditional end to British rule and called for a united mass struggle toward complete independence. The very name of the conference, “Anti-Compromise”, reflects its foundational rejection of any negotiated settlement or tactical accommodation with the colonial government.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs correctly matches a place with an event associated with the Forward Bloc and related nationalist activities?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Moirang : First hoisting of the Free India flag on Indian soil by the INA

questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correctly matched: Moirang, a town in present-day Manipur, holds an iconic place in the history of the Indian National Army (INA). On 14 April 1944, Colonel Shaukat Malik of the INA hoisted the flag of Azad Hind (Free India) at Moirang, marking the first time the INA’s tricolour was raised on Indian soil. This was a defining moment in Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose’s military campaign against British rule, as the INA, advancing alongside Japanese forces, had penetrated Indian territory during the Imphal-Kohima campaign. Though the INA’s advance was ultimately halted, the hoisting of the flag at Moirang remains a powerful symbol of the INA’s determination to liberate India.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched: The Forward Bloc was not formed in Saigon. It was founded on 3 May 1939 in India, initially as a left-wing consolidation platform within the Congress. Saigon (presentday Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam) has no direct association with the formation of the Forward Bloc.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched: The Anti-Compromise Conference was held at Ramgarh (present-day Jharkhand) in March 1940, not Bangkok. Bangkok is associated with the broader Southeast Asian network of the Indian independence movement, particularly the Indian Independence League activities during World War II.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched: The famous INA trials were held at the Red Fort, Delhi, beginning in November 1945, where INA officers, including Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal, and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, were tried for treason. Nagpur is associated with the 1940 Forward Bloc conference, where the party declared itself socialist and adopted the slogan “All Power to the Indian People,” not with the INA trials.

questions.q: The federal scheme proposed under the Government of India Act, 1935, failed primarily because:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: The princely states refused to join the federation
options.C: The British Parliament repealed the Act before its implementation
options.D: The Muslim League opposed the federation

questions.explanation:
The Government of India Act, 1935 was the most elaborate constitutional instrument enacted for British India and envisaged a two-tier structure, an All-India Federation at the centre, linking both the British Indian provinces and the princely states, alongside provincial autonomy at the lower level. However, while the provincial autonomy provisions came into operation and elections were held in 1937, the federal scheme at the centre never came into effect, and the primary reason was the refusal of the princely states to accede to the proposed federation.

The Act stipulated that the federation would come into existence only when princely states representing at least 50% of the total population of all states and holding 52 out of 104 seats in the proposed Council of States (upper house) had signed Instruments of Accession. The accession of princely states was made voluntary, which proved to be the fatal flaw. The princes were deeply apprehensive about surrendering their sovereignty and autonomy and they feared loss of their special privileges, interference in their internal administration, and being subjected to a legislature where elected representatives of British India would dominate. Encouraged by the Chamber of Princes and wary of growing nationalist sentiment, the princely states collectively stalled, and the required number of accessions never materialised.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs of Gandhian Movements and their Significance: 1. Champaran Satyagraha : First Civil Disobedience movement by Gandhi in India 2. Ahmedabad Mill Strike : First hunger strike undertaken by Gandhi 3. Kheda Satyagraha : First Non-Cooperation movement How many pairs of the given above are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correct: The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) is regarded as Gandhi’s first experiment with civil disobedience in India, where he defied the government’s order to leave the area.

Pair 2 is correct: During the Ahmedabad Mill Workers’ Strike (1918), Gandhi undertook his first fast unto death to support the workers’ demand for higher wages. Pair 3 is correct: The Kheda Satyagraha (1918) is often regarded as the first Non-Cooperation movement because peasants collectively refused to pay revenue taxes to the colonial government.

questions.q: With reference to the formation of Congress ministries in 1937, consider the following statements: 1. Congress initially refused to form ministries because of the Governor’s discretionary powers. 2. Congress ministries remained in office for nearly 28 months. 3. Congress immediately accepted office after the election results were declared. How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Despite winning clear majorities in several provinces in the February 1937 elections, Congress initially refused to assume office and did not immediately form ministries. The central point of contention was the special powers and discretionary authority vested in the Governors under the Government of India Act, 1935. Congress objected particularly to Section 93, which empowered Governors to take over provincial administration, and to the broader range of the Governor’s special responsibilities that allowed intervention in ministerial functioning without legislative accountability. Congress demanded assurances that Governors would not use these powers to override or obstruct elected ministries. This deadlock persisted for several months until the British government, through a clarificatory statement by the Secretary of State for India, Lord Zetland, indicated that Governors would not ordinarily interfere with day-to-day ministerial functioning. Satisfied with this assurance, though the constitutional powers themselves remained unchanged, Congress agreed to take office, and ministries were formed beginning in July 1937.

Statement 2 is correct: Congress ministries functioned from July 1937 until October–November 1939, a period of approximately 28 months. Their resignation was triggered by the outbreak of World War II in September 1939, when Viceroy Lord Linlithgow unilaterally declared India a belligerent nation without consulting Indian political leadership or the elected provincial legislatures. Congress demanded a clear British commitment to Indian independence as a condition for cooperation in the war effort. When no satisfactory response was forthcoming, the Congress Working Committee directed all Congress ministries to resign, which they did by November 1939, bringing the brief but significant experiment of provincial self-governance to an end.

Statement 3 is incorrect: As established above, Congress emphatically did not immediately accept office after the election results were declared in February 1937. A gap of approximately four to five months elapsed between the declaration of results and the actual formation of Congress ministries in July 1937, during which sustained negotiations and correspondence took place between Congress leadership and the British authorities over the Governor’s special powers. This period of deliberate refusal was itself a significant political statement by Congress, demonstrating its unwillingness to function as a mere administrative instrument under a constitutional framework that it fundamentally disagreed with, unless adequate assurances of genuine responsible government were provided.

questions.q: The Congress ministries resigned in 1939 for which one of the following reasons?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.B: India was declared a participant in WWII without consultation

questions.explanation:
The Congress ministries resigned in OctoberNovember 1939 primarily because Viceroy Lord Linlithgow unilaterally declared India a participant in World War II on 3 September 1939, without consulting the elected Congress ministries functioning in the provinces or the broader Indian political leadership. Congress regarded this as a grave constitutional affront, a stark demonstration that despite the exercise of provincial autonomy under the Government of India Act, 1935, India’s fundamental political status remained that of a colonial dependency whose most consequential decisions, including the question of war and peace, were made entirely at British discretion without any reference to Indian representatives or popular will.

The Congress Working Committee, meeting in September 1939, passed a resolution demanding that Britain clearly define its war aims specifically, whether the war was being fought for democracy and self-determination, and further demanded a concrete commitment to Indian independence as the price of Congress’s cooperation in the war effort. When Viceroy Linlithgow’s response in October 1939 proved unsatisfactory, offering only a vague promise of post-war consultations and a possible review of the 1935 Act rather than any firm commitment to independence, the Congress Working Committee directed all Congress provincial ministries to resign. By November 1939, all eight Congress ministries had tendered their resignations, bringing approximately 28 months of Congress provincial governance to an abrupt end.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the Lahore Resolution (1940) is incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct

options.A: It came to be popularly known as the Pakistan Resolution.
options.B: It was moved by Fazlul Huq.
options.C: Sikandar Hayat Khan was associated with it.

questions.explanation:
Statement A is correct: Despite the absence of the word in the text, the resolution came to be universally known as the Pakistan Resolution due to its political implication of a separate Muslim homeland.

Statement B is correct: The resolution was formally moved by A. K. Fazlul Huq, the Krishak Praja Party leader and Chief Minister of Bengal, at the Lahore Session of the Muslim League on 23 March 1940.

Statement C is correct: Sir Sikandar Hayat Khan, leader of the Punjab Unionist Party, was associated with the resolution, having played a role in shaping an early draft. However, he later distanced himself from more rigid separatist interpretations, maintaining that the proposal envisaged a loose federal arrangement rather than outright partition.

Statement D is incorrect: The Lahore Resolution of March 1940 notably never used the word “Pakistan” anywhere in its text. The resolution referred instead to geographically contiguous Muslim majority units in the northwestern and eastern zones of India being constituted into “independent states” with full autonomy and sovereignty. The specific term “Pakistan,” coined earlier by Choudhry Rahmat Ali in his 1933 pamphlet Now or Never, was entirely absent from the official language. The popular label “Pakistan Resolution” emerged later through political discourse and press usage rather than as the League’s formal terminology. Jinnah and the Muslim League initially preferred this deliberate ambiguity, as the phrase “independent states,” particularly in the plural, permitted multiple interpretations and helped consolidate wider Muslim political support.

questions.q: Consider the following international developments: 1. Atlantic Charter 2. Japanese military advance in Asia 3. Pressure from Roosevelt and Chiang Kai-shek Which of the above developments contributed to the increased pressure on Britain to negotiate with Indian leaders in 1941–42?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Atlantic Charter (1941) was a joint declaration issued by Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt in August 1941, affirming among other principles the right of all peoples to choose their own form of government and the restoration of self-government to those forcibly deprived of it. Indian nationalists and American opinion immediately interpreted this as applicable to India, placing Churchill in the uncomfortable position of having to explain why a charter proclaimed in the name of democracy and self-determination did not extend to Britain’s largest colony. This created significant ideological pressure and international embarrassment for Britain.

Japanese military advances in Asia dramatically transformed the strategic situation. Following Japan’s entry into the war after Pearl Harbour in December 1941, Japanese forces rapidly overran Malaya, Singapore, Burma, and were advancing toward the Indian border by early 1942. The fall of Singapore in February 1942, described by Churchill as the worst military disaster in British history, made Indian cooperation in the war effort a matter of urgent strategic necessity rather than a political preference. Britain needed Indian soldiers, resources, and active nationalist support, not sullen colonial acquiescence.

Pressure from Roosevelt and Chiang Kai-shek added crucial external diplomatic weight. American President Roosevelt was genuinely committed to anti-colonialism and repeatedly pressed Churchill to resolve the Indian political deadlock, viewing Indian cooperation as essential to the Allied war effort in Asia. Chinese Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek visited India in early 1942 and publicly appealed to Indian leaders to support the Allied cause while simultaneously urging Britain to grant India genuine political freedom, an intervention that further embarrassed Britain internationally and reinforced American pressure on Churchill to send a credible political mission to India.

questions.q: The Kheda Satyagraha of 1918 was primarily launched against:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Forced cultivation of indigo by European planters
options.B: Heavy taxation despite crop failure caused by drought
options.C: The Rowlatt Act was imposed by the British Government
options.D: Reduction in wages of textile mill workers

questions.explanation:
The Kheda Satyagraha was launched in 1918 in Gujarat after a severe drought caused crop failure, and peasants demanded remission of land revenue.

The British government refused to suspend revenue collection despite the poor agricultural conditions of the farmers.

Mahatma Gandhi advised the peasants not to pay taxes until their demands were accepted.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding underground leadership and resistance during the Quit India Movement: 1. Jayaprakash Narayan escaped from Hazaribagh jail. 2. Aruna Asaf Ali played a major role in organising underground resistance. 3. Sucheta Kripalani was associated with underground organisational work. 4. Rajendra Prasad led the secret Congress Radio operations. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Jayaprakash Narayan made a dramatic escape from Hazaribagh Central Jail in November 1942 along with several other political prisoners. After his escape, JP became one of the most active underground leaders of the movement, coordinating resistance networks and even attempting to link the Indian struggle with Allied anti-fascist forces operating in Nepal and beyond.

Statement 2 is correct: Aruna Asaf Ali became one of the most celebrated figures of the Quit India Movement. She famously hoisted the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan on 9 August 1942 after senior leaders were arrested, and subsequently went underground to organise resistance networks across the country. She was widely hailed as the “Heroine of the 1942 Movement.”

Statement 3 is correct: Sucheta Kripalani actively participated in underground organisational work during the movement, working alongside other resistance leaders to sustain agitation despite the comprehensive suppression of overt political activity by British authorities.

Statement 4 is incorrect: The underground Congress Radio was operated by Usha Mehta, not Rajendra Prasad. Mehta ran clandestine broadcasts from secret locations in Bombay, keeping nationalist sentiment alive until the transmitter was eventually traced and shut down by British authorities. Rajendra Prasad had been arrested and was not associated with radio operations.

questions.q: Which of the following contributed to the Bengal Famine of 1943? 1. Scorched earth policy in coastal Bengal 2. Diversion of food supplies for war purposes 3. Hoarding and profiteering Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
All three factors contributed to the Bengal Famine of 1943, which claimed an estimated 2 to 3 million lives and remains one of the gravest humanitarian disasters of colonial India.

The scorched earth policy was implemented by British authorities in coastal Bengal to deny resources to a potentially advancing Japanese army. Under the “boat denial” and “rice denial” policies, boats were confiscated or destroyed, and rice stocks were removed from vulnerable coastal areas. This severely disrupted local transport and food distribution networks on which Bengal’s rural economy depended, creating acute shortages even before the famine fully developed.

The diversion of food supplies for war purposes was another major structural factor. Wartime priorities required provisioning Allied military operations in the broader Southeast Asian theatre, while shipping constraints sharply limited imports. Despite repeated appeals from Indian officials, adequate relief shipments were not arranged in time, worsening the crisis.

Hoarding and profiteering significantly intensified the famine. As supply uncertainty and panic spread, traders and merchants hoarded grain in anticipation of rising prices, reducing market availability and driving food prices beyond the reach of the rural poor, whose purchasing power had collapsed. This aligns with Amartya Sen’s analysis of the famine as an entitlement failure, where food availability alone did not determine famine conditions; access to food was the decisive issue.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs of military formations of the Indian National Army (INA) and their commanding officers: 1. Subhas Brigade : Shah Nawaz Khan 2. Gandhi Brigade : Inayat Kiani 3. Nehru Brigade : Prem Kumar Sahgal 4. Bahadur Group : Shaukat Malik How many pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correctly matched: The 1st Guerrilla Regiment (Subhas Brigade) was commanded by Colonel Shah Nawaz Khan, so this pairing is correct.

Pair 2 is correctly matched: The 2nd Guerrilla Regiment (Gandhi Brigade) was under Colonel Inayat Kiani, making this pair correct.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched: The Nehru Brigade was commanded by Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, not Prem Kumar Sahgal. Sahgal held other important military responsibilities within the INA, but pairing him with the Nehru Brigade is incorrect.

Pair 4 is correctly matched: Colonel Shaukat Hayat Malik commanded the Bahadur Group, the INA’s specialised commando and intelligence unit tasked with reconnaissance, infiltration, and sabotage behind enemy lines. A unit of the Bahadur Group under his leadership entered Moirang in Manipur in April 1944, where the Azad Hind flag was hoisted for the first time on Indian soil.

Additional facts: • The INA’s 1st Division was structurally organised and placed under the direct operational command of Major General Mohammad Zaman Kiani. • The Subhas Brigade actively participated in the Japanese U-Go offensive, specifically engaging British colonial forces in the Chin Hills and Kohima sectors. • Colonel Shaukat Malik’s Bahadur Group successfully penetrated Indian territory and officially hoisted the Indian tricolor at Moirang in Manipur on April 14, 1944. • The Rani of Jhansi Regiment was formally raised in July 1943 in Singapore, functioning strictly as an all-female frontline combat infantry unit. • Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan commanded the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, with Janaki Thevar serving prominently as her second-in-command. • Subhas Chandra Bose officially established the Supreme Command of the INA at Singapore before relocating its forward operational headquarters to Rangoon in January 1944. • The British colonial administration captured INA officers Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal, and G. S. Dhillon, subjecting them to the historic public treason trials at the Red Fort in November 1945. • The Indian National Congress explicitly organised the INA Defence Committee, strategically utilising prominent legal stalwarts like Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, and K. N. Katju for the defence. • The Royal Indian Navy mutiny in February 1946 was directly catalysed by the explosive political atmosphere generated by the INA trials and the glorification of these specific brigades.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Desai-Liaquat Pact: 1. It proposed parity between Congress and the Muslim League in the interim government. 2. It was officially ratified by both Congress and the Muslim League. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Desai-Liaquat Pact (January 1945), negotiated between Bhulabhai Desai, the Congress leader in the Central Legislative Assembly, and Liaquat Ali Khan of the Muslim League, proposed the formation of an interim central government with parity between Congress and the Muslim League. Under the proposal, both Congress and the League were to receive 40 percent representation each, while the remaining 20 percent would be allocated to minorities and other groups.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The pact never received formal approval from either the Congress or the Muslim League. Although the negotiations generated initial interest, both sides later distanced themselves from it. Jinnah denied that Liaquat Ali Khan had authority to conclude such an agreement on behalf of the League, while the Congress leadership, including Gandhi, did not officially endorse Desai’s initiative, as it had been undertaken without formal authorisation. Consequently, the arrangement remained an unofficial political understanding that collapsed without implementation.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Kheda Satyagraha became an important peasant movement under Mahatma Gandhi. Reason (R): The British government agreed to suspend tax collection and return confiscated property to the peasants. Select the correct answer:
questions.question_type: Assertion and Reason — Standard Relationship Evaluation

options.A: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.B: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.explanation:
Assertion (A) is true: The Kheda Satyagraha emerged as a significant peasant movement led by Mahatma Gandhi in 1918 against unjust revenue demands.

Reason (R) is true: The British government ultimately agreed to suspend tax collection for the affected period, reduce revenue enhancement and return confiscated property.

The success of these demands strengthened the movement and demonstrated the effectiveness of Gandhian satyagraha; therefore, R correctly explains A.

questions.q: Which of the following INA officers commanded the 2nd Infantry Regiment during the Mount Popa campaign in Burma?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The 2nd Infantry Regiment, under Colonel Prem Kumar Sahgal, was assigned defensive responsibilities at Mount Popa during the later phase of the Burma Campaign. Sahgal, who also served as one of Bose’s senior military associates, commanded the regiment during these operations.

Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon did not command the 2nd Infantry Regiment. He was associated with the Nehru Brigade (4th Guerrilla Regiment), and during the retreat phase, surviving INA elements from different formations came into overlapping operational contact, but command of the Mount Popa defensive position rested with Sahgal.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs regarding the allocation of portfolios in the Interim Government of 1946: 1. Sardar Baldev Singh : Defence 2. Joginder Nath Mandal : Labour 3. H. Bhabha : Works, Mines and Power 4. Ghazanfar Ali Khan : Communications How many pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correctly matched: Baldev Singh held the Defence portfolio.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched: Jogendra Nath Mandal held the Law portfolio, not Labour. Labour was held by Jagjivan Ram.

Pair 3 is correctly matched: C. H. Bhabha held the Works, Mines and Power portfolio.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched: Ghazanfar Ali Khan held the Health portfolio, not Communications. Communications was held by Abdur Rab Nishtar.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly in December 1946: 1. The Muslim League boycotted the proceedings. 2. Sachchidananda Sinha served as the temporary President of the Assembly. 3. The Constitution of India was formally adopted during this inaugural session. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Muslim League boycotted the inaugural session of the Constituent Assembly held on 9 December 1946, refusing to participate on the grounds that the Cabinet Mission Plan’s grouping scheme had not been accepted in the form the League insisted upon. This boycott meant the Constituent Assembly began its proceedings without the League’s participation, significantly undermining its claim to be a fully representative body.

Statement 2 is correct: Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member of the Assembly, served as its temporary (pro tem) President during the inaugural session, in accordance with established parliamentary convention of the senior-most member presiding over initial proceedings. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was subsequently elected as the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The Constitution was emphatically not adopted during the inaugural session of December 1946. The Constituent Assembly took nearly three years of deliberations to complete its work, formally adopting the Constitution of India on 26 November 1949, which came into effect on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: Who was appointed as the final Viceroy following Attlee’s Declaration?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Lord Louis Mountbatten was appointed as the last Viceroy of India following Attlee’s Declaration of 20 February 1947, replacing Lord Wavell, who had been considered insufficiently effective in resolving the final constitutional deadlock. Mountbatten arrived in India in March 1947 and moved with notable speed, advancing the transfer of power deadline from June 1948 to August 1947.

Mountbatten announced the Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) on 3 June 1947, which formally accepted partition as the basis for the transfer of power and provided for the creation of two independent dominions, India and Pakistan. The Indian Independence Act was subsequently passed by the British Parliament in July 1947, and power was transferred on 14–15 August 1947.

Mountbatten then served as the first GovernorGeneral of independent India until June 1948, after which he was succeeded by C. Rajagopalachari.

questions.q: Which of the following leaders was not associated with the Kheda Satyagraha? 1. Narahari Parikh 2. Ravi Shankar Vyas 3. Subhas Chandra Bose 4. Mohanlal Pandya Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: Narahari Parikh was one of the devoted Gandhians who actively participated in organising villagers during the Kheda Satyagraha.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Ravi Shankar Vyas was associated with Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel in providing leadership during the movement.

Statement 3 is correct: Subhas Chandra Bose was not associated with the Kheda Satyagraha of 1918.

Statement 4 is incorrect: Mohanlal Pandya played an important role in mobilising peasants during the Kheda movement.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the integration of princely states after independence: 1. Accession to India automatically deprived princely rulers of all internal autonomy with immediate effect. 2. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon played a central role in the process of integration. 3. The Instrument of Accession covered Defence, External Affairs, and Communications. 4. Standstill Agreements were used to maintain existing administrative arrangements temporarily. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: Accession to India did not immediately deprive princely rulers of all internal autonomy. The initial Instrument of Accession was deliberately limited in scope, rulers retained internal sovereignty and administrative control over their states. The full integration and merger of princely states into the Indian Union was a gradual process that unfolded in phases after accession, with complete administrative integration and the eventual abolition of privy purses coming much later.

Statement 2 is correct: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of States, and V. P. Menon, as Secretary of the States Ministry, were the principal architects of the integration of princely states. Through a combination of persuasion, political pressure, and, in the case of Hyderabad, military action (Operation Polo, 1948), they successfully secured the accession of nearly all 565 princely states, one of the most remarkable feats of political consolidation in modern history.

Statement 3 is correct: The Instrument of Accession was deliberately kept narrow, covering only three subjects, Defence, External Affairs, and Communications, to make it easier for princes to sign without feeling they were surrendering complete sovereignty immediately. This strategic minimalism was central to Patel and Menon’s success in securing rapid accessions.

Statement 4 is correct: Standstill Agreements were signed alongside the Instruments of Accession to ensure that existing administrative, commercial, and communication arrangements between the princely states and the former British Indian government continued functioning without disruption during the transition period, providing practical continuity while the larger question of full integration was worked out.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the Boundary Commissions set up in 1947 is incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct

options.A: Sir Cyril Radcliffe, a British legal expert with no prior experience in India, was appointed as the common chairman of both Boundary Commissions.
options.B: Each commission consisted of four High Court judges, with equal representation from Congress and the Muslim League.
options.C: The final boundary awards were officially made public before independence so that territorial boundaries were clearly settled in advance.
options.D: The Bengal Boundary Commission also had to determine the territorial disposition of Sylhet following the referendum held there.

questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Sir Cyril Radcliffe had never visited India before his appointment and was selected precisely because he was considered an impartial legal figure without prior political associations in the subcontinent.

Statement 2 is correct: The Punjab Boundary Commission and the Bengal Boundary Commission each consisted of four High Court judges, two nominated by the Congress and two by the Muslim League, with Radcliffe serving as the common chairman.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The boundary awards were deliberately withheld until after independence and were announced only on 17 August 1947, two days after the transfer of power. Mountbatten’s decision to delay publication was intended to ensure that the immediate political consequences of the award would be handled by the new governments rather than the departing British administration. This delay has been widely criticised because it denied administrators and populations prior clarity regarding territorial allocation, thereby aggravating the disorder and communal violence accompanying partition.

Statement 4 is correct: The Sylhet referendum, held in July 1947, resulted in a vote in favour of joining East Pakistan, after which the Bengal Boundary process determined the final territorial demarcation relating to the district.

questions.q: Who among the following were the members of the Cabinet Mission sent to India in March 1946? 1. Lord Pethick-Lawrence 2. Sir Stafford Cripps 3. V. Alexander 4. Lord Wavell Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Cabinet Mission of 1946 comprised three members of the British Cabinet: Lord PethickLawrence (Secretary of State for India), Sir Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade), and A. V. Alexander (First Lord of the Admiralty). All three arrived in India in March 1946 to negotiate a framework for the transfer of power.

Lord Wavell, as Viceroy of India, was present during the Cabinet Mission negotiations and played a facilitative role in the discussions, but he was not a member of the Cabinet Mission itself. His position was that of the Crown’s representative in India rather than a member of the Westminster Cabinet delegation. This distinction is constitutionally significant, the Mission was explicitly a delegation of British Cabinet ministers sent to negotiate India’s constitutional future, a role entirely separate from Wavell’s viceregal functions. Wavell was eventually replaced by Lord Mountbatten as Viceroy in March 1947, as the British government felt a fresh political approach was needed to finalise the transfer of power.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the main proposal put forward under the Wavell Plan to break the constitutional deadlock?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Reconstitution of a sovereign Constituent Assembly to frame India’s Constitution
