options.B: Complete Indianisation of the Viceroy’s Executive Council, except for the Viceroy and the Commander-in-Chief
options.C: Immediate acceptance of the demand for Pakistan as a separate sovereign state
options.D: Abolition of the office of the Governor-General and transfer of authority to an interim national government

questions.explanation:
The Wavell Plan (June 1945), announced by Viceroy Lord Wavell in connection with the Simla Conference, proposed the reconstitution of the Viceroy’s Executive Council through near-complete Indianisation. All members, except the Viceroy and the Commander-in-Chief, were to be Indians. The plan also proposed parity between caste Hindus and Muslims in the reconstituted council, while the External Affairs portfolio was to be transferred, for the first time, to an Indian member.

The Simla Conference (June–July 1945), convened to operationalise this plan, ultimately failed because of the unresolved issue of Muslim representation. Muhammad Ali Jinnah insisted that all Muslim members of the Executive Council must be nominated solely by the Muslim League, thereby reinforcing the League’s claim that it alone represented India’s Muslims. Congress rejected this, as it included Muslim members within its own fold and refused to concede the League’s exclusive representative status.

As no compromise could be reached, Wavell suspended the conference without agreement, marking another major constitutional deadlock.

questions.q: Under the Poona Pact, the number of seats reserved for the Depressed Classes in provincial legislatures was increased to:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Poona Pact increased the number of reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in provincial legislatures from 71, as proposed under the Communal Award, to 148.

Thus, although separate electorates were abandoned, the Pact expanded political representation for the Depressed Classes within the framework of joint electorates.

The Pact also reserved 18% of seats allotted to the general electorate in the Central Legislature for the Depressed Classes.

questions.q: Subhas Chandra Bose escaped from India in 1941 under which of the following aliases?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Subhas Chandra Bose made his famous “Great Escape” in January 1941 from his residence at Elgin Road, Calcutta, where he had been kept under British surveillance following imprisonment and house arrest. Disguised as “Muhammad Ziauddin,” a Pathan insurance agent, he successfully evaded British intelligence and slipped out of Calcutta.

From there, Bose travelled to Peshawar, aided by underground nationalist networks, including associates linked to the Forward Bloc. He then crossed into Afghanistan, reaching Kabul, where efforts were made to establish contact with Axis representatives. Subsequently, adopting the identity of “Orlando Mazzotta,” presented as an Italian, he secured passage onward. From Kabul, he travelled through the Soviet Union and eventually reached Berlin in April 1941.

In Germany, Bose established the Free India Centre and organised the Indian Legion from Indian prisoners of war captured by Axis forces in the North African campaign.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs related to developments within the Indian National Congress in 1939: 1. Govind Ballabh Pant Resolution : Restricted Bose’s freedom in forming the Working Committee 2. Tripuri Session : Jawaharlal Nehru became Congress President 3. Bose’s resignation : Rajendra Prasad became Congress President Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correctly matched: The Govind Ballabh Pant Resolution, moved at the Tripuri Session, effectively stripped Bose of his presidential autonomy by requiring him to constitute the Working Committee in accordance with the wishes of Mahatma Gandhi. Rather than strengthening his position as the newly re-elected president, this resolution rendered Bose’s authority largely ceremonial, as most senior Gandhian leaders refused to serve under him. It was a decisive organisational blow that made Bose’s continued functioning as president untenable.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched: At the Tripuri Session, Subhas Chandra Bose was re-elected as Congress President after defeating Pattabhi Sitaramayya, not Jawaharlal Nehru. Nehru had previously served as Congress President at the Lucknow (1936) and Faizpur (1937) Sessions and was not a presidential candidate at Tripuri.

Pair 3 is correctly matched: Following Bose’s resignation from the Congress presidency in April 1939, unable to function effectively under the constraints imposed by the Pant Resolution and facing continued opposition from the Gandhian majority, Rajendra Prasad was elected as Congress President in his place. Prasad was a trusted member of Gandhi’s inner circle, and his election signalled the complete restoration of Gandhian dominance within the Congress organisation following the turbulent Tripuri episode.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding temple entry movements in pre-independence India: 1. The Guruvayur Satyagraha was associated with K. Kelappan. 2. The Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 was issued in Travancore. 3. The Temple Entry Proclamation opened temples to all castes in the Madras Presidency. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Guruvayur Satyagraha of 1931–32 was centrally associated with K. Kelappan, a prominent social reformer and Congress leader from Kerala, widely revered as the “Kerala Gandhi.” The Guruvayur temple, located in the present-day Thrissur district of Kerala, was then part of the Malabar region under the Madras Presidency. Kelappan led the satyagraha demanding the right of entry for lower-caste Hindus who were traditionally excluded from the temple. When the demand was not met, he undertook a fast-untodeath at the temple premises in September 1932. Gandhi himself persuaded Kelappan to break his fast, arguing that broader social conditions were not yet ripe for the sacrifice. Though the satyagraha did not immediately succeed in opening the Guruvayur temple, it generated widespread public debate and significantly energised the broader temple entry movement across Kerala and India.

Statement 2 is correct: The landmark Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 was issued by the princely state of Travancore, under Maharaja Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma, on 12 November 1936. This historic proclamation declared that all Hindu temples under state jurisdiction would be open to all Hindus, irrespective of caste, effectively ending centuries of institutionalised exclusion of lower castes from places of worship. It was a pioneering act, the first such state-level proclamation in India and was widely hailed by Gandhi and nationalist leaders. The proclamation was significantly influenced by sustained social reform movements in Kerala, including those led by Sree Narayana Guru and the prolonged agitations of the Ezhava and other communities.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 applied exclusively to Travancore, which was an independent princely state, and did not extend to the Madras Presidency, which was directly administered British territory. The two were entirely separate jurisdictions. Temple entry in Madras Presidency was a distinct and more prolonged struggle; notably, the Madras Temple Entry Authorisation Act was passed only in 1947, enabling lower-caste Hindus to enter temples in that region. Thus, conflating the 1936 Travancore Proclamation with the Madras Presidency represents a fundamental geographical and administrative inaccuracy.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Meerut Conspiracy Case: 1. The colonial authorities conducted the judicial proceedings in Bombay to ensure a standard trial by jury. 2. The colonial administration successfully prevented any British nationals from being indicted in this specific trial. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: The colonial government deliberately shifted the trial venue from Bombay to Meerut specifically to deny the accused the legal right to a jury trial.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The British did not prevent their own nationals from being indicted; three British communists, Philip Spratt, Ben Bradley, and Lester Hutchinson, were prominently arrested and tried alongside the Indian activists.

Additional facts: • The arrests were executed in March 1929, and the formal charge against the accused was filed under Section 121A of the Indian Penal Code. • The prosecution accused the leaders of conspiring to deprive the King-Emperor of the sovereignty of British India. 3 Prominent Indian communist leaders arrested included S. A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmad, P. C. Joshi, and Shaukat Usmani. • A Central Defence Committee was formed by the Indian National Congress to fight the case legally. • Jawaharlal Nehru, M. A. Ansari, and M. C. Chagla actively served as defence lawyers for the accused activists. • The judicial proceedings lasted for three and a half years, becoming the most expensive trial in British India. • The trial attracted massive international condemnation from prominent global figures, including Albert Einstein and Romain Rolland. • In early 1933, twenty-seven accused individuals were convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment or transportation. • Muzaffar Ahmed, S. A. Dange, Joglekar, Philip Spratt, Ben Bradley, and Shaukat Usmani were among those convicted.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Rowlatt Act (1919): 1. The Rowlatt Act was officially known as the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act. 2. The Act was based on the recommendations of the Rowlatt Commission headed by Sir Sidney Rowlatt. 3. Under the Act, political activists could be detained without trial. 4. Mohammed Ali Jinnah and Madan Mohan Malaviya supported the Act in the Imperial Legislative Council. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Rowlatt Act, passed in March 1919, was officially called the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act.

Statement 2 is correct: The Act was based on the recommendations of the Rowlatt Commission, headed by British judge Sir Sidney Rowlatt, which investigated revolutionary and nationalist activities in India.

Statement 3 is correct: The Act empowered the government to arrest and imprison political activists without trial and allowed secret trials without legal assistance.

Statement 4 is incorrect: Indian leaders such as Mohammed Ali Jinnah, Madan Mohan Malaviya and Mazhar-ul-Haq opposed the Act and resigned from the Imperial Legislative Council in protest.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Tebhaga Movement: 1. The provincial legislature successfully enacted the Bargadars Bill to permanently secure tenant cultivation rights. 2. The Land Revenue Commission explicitly recommended granting a two-thirds crop share to the cultivating sharecroppers. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: Although the Muslim League ministry led by H. S. Suhrawardy introduced the Bargadars Bill to pacify the agitation, the legislation was heavily diluted and ultimately aborted due to intense political lobbying by powerful landlords.

Statement 2 is correct: The Land Revenue Commission of Bengal, formally known as the Floud Commission, had officially recommended in 1940 that the legal share of the harvest for sharecroppers should be increased to two-thirds.

Additional facts: • The Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha officially launched the massive agrarian struggle in 1946. • Sharecroppers, locally identified as bargadars or adhiars, customarily surrendered half of their total agricultural yield to the jotedars (landlords). • The central rallying slogans of the agitation were “Tebhaga chai” (we want two-thirds) and “Nij khamare dhan tolo” (store the paddy in our own granaries). • The protesting peasants systematically refused to transport the newly harvested paddy to the traditional jotedar storage facilities (khamars). • The Dinajpur district in northern Bengal emerged as the primary epicentre of the fiercest physical confrontations. • Prominent communist and peasant leaders, including Bhowani Sen, Sunil Sen, and Moni Singh, actively directed the regional grassroots mobilisations. • The movement recorded massive structural participation from marginalised Rajbanshi tribal communities and impoverished Namasudra peasants. • Peasant women independently formed organised self-defence squads known as Nari Bahinis to physically resist armed police raids and landlord retainers. • Escalating communal violence in Noakhali and the impending geopolitical partition of Bengal severely fractured the movement’s demographic solidarity and momentum by mid-1947.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs of early trade unions and their associated founding leaders: 1. Bombay Mill and Millhands’ Association : N.M. Lokhande 2. Madras Labour Union : B.P. Wadia 3. Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association : Mahatma Gandhi 4. All India Trade Union Congress: J.L. Nehru How many pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correct: Narayan Meghaji Lokhande founded the Bombay Mill and Millhands’ Association in 1890, which acted as a philanthropic clearinghouse for workers’ grievances.

Pair 2 is correct: B. P. Wadia established the Madras Labour Union in 1918, historically recognised as the first modern, formally organised trade union in India.

Pair 3 is correct: Mahatma Gandhi founded the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (Majdoor Mahajan Sabha) in 1920, following the successful implementation of his trusteeship model during the 1918 mill strike.

Pair 4 is incorrect: The AITUC was founded by N. M. Joshi, Lala Lajpat Rai, and others in 1920. Jawaharlal Nehru was not the founding leader (though he presided over it much later in 1929)

Additional facts: • Sorabji Shapoorji Bengali unsuccessfully attempted to introduce a pioneering legislative bill in the Bombay Legislative Council in 1878 to formally regulate industrial working conditions. • N. M. Lokhande launched the prominent Anglo-Marathi weekly journal Dinabandhu in 1880, specifically to highlight severe labour exploitation and organise mill workers. • The first Indian Factory Act of 1881 primarily focused on regulating child labour, explicitly prohibiting the industrial employment of children under the age of seven. • The subsequent Indian Factory Act of 1891 officially guaranteed a weekly holiday for all factory workers and strictly fixed working hours for women. • The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was explicitly established in October 1920 to secure an organised, recognised labour representation delegation at the newly formed International Labour Organisation (ILO). • Diwan Chaman Lall was officially appointed as the first General Secretary of the All India Trade Union Congress during its inaugural Bombay session. • The landmark Indian Trade Union Act of 1926 formally recognised registered trade unions as legal corporate bodies, granting them specific immunities from civil and criminal prosecution. • Moderate labour leaders, prominently including N. M. Joshi and V. V. Giri formally seceded from the AITUC during the 1929 Nagpur session to establish the independent Indian Trades Union Federation (ITUF). • A radical communist faction further splintered from the AITUC in 1931, subsequently establishing the militant Red Trade Union Congress under the direct leadership of B. T. Ranadive and S. V. Deshpande. • The Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC) was formally inaugurated in May 1947 by mainstream nationalist leaders, including Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, to counter growing communist dominance in the labour sector. • Add that N. M. Lokhande submitted the Charter of Demands to Lord Ripon (Viceroy of India) in 1890, which included demands for an 8-hour working day, a weekly holiday, and a minimum wage.

questions.q: Match List-I with List-II List-I (Organisations) List-II (Associated Leaders) a. Rajkot Praja Mandal 1. Swami Ramanand Tirtha b. Mysore State Congress 2. K.T. Bhashyam c. Hyderabad State Congress 3. U.N. Dhebar d. Orissa State’s Conference 4. Sarangadhar Das Select the correct answer using the codes given below: a b c d
questions.question_type: Match the Following — Two-List Matching — Answer-Code Matrix
questions.explanation:
U. N. Dhebar was a prominent leader in the Rajkot Prajamandal movement against excessive taxation and administrative decline in the Rajkot princely state. Sardar Patel also led the Rajkot Satyagraha (1938) with Dhebar’s support.

K. T. Bhashyam was a close associate of Gandhiji who led satyagraha in Mysore in 1939.

Swami Ramanand Tirtha was the most prominent leader of the Hyderabad State Congress (established 1938).

Sarangadhar Das served as General Secretary of the Orissa State People’s Conference from 1937 to 1946 and was President of the Orissa and C. P. States Regional Council from 1946 to 1947.

Additional facts: • Swami Ramanand Tirtha: He was the President of Hyderabad State Congress and led the struggle against the Nizam’s autocratic rule. • U. N. Dhebar: He later became President of the Indian National Congress (1955–1959). • Sarngadhar Das: He was elected to India’s Constituent Assembly and was a Member of Parliament belonging to the Socialist Party. • Rajkot Satyagraha: In 1939, Gandhiji entrusted Vallabhbhai Patel to lead the satyagraha in Rajkot, marking the first time Gandhi tried his specific techniques of controlled mass struggle in a native state.

questions.q: Which one of the following was not associated with the legislative record of Congress ministries (1937–39)?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Introduction of Permanent Settlement was not part of the legislative record of Congress ministries (1937-39) for the straightforward reason that the Permanent Settlement had already been introduced over 140 years earlier, by Governor-General Lord Cornwallis in 1793.

It was a revenue arrangement that permanently fixed the land revenue demand of the British government from zamindars in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, effectively converting zamindars into hereditary proprietors with fixed tax obligations.

questions.q: Who among the following founded the Bihar Kisan Sabha?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Swami Sahajanand Saraswati founded the Bihar Kisan Sabha to organise peasants against zamindari exploitation and agrarian injustices.

He advocated the abolition of the zamindari system and the transfer of ownership rights to cultivators.

Due to his dedicated service towards peasants, he became popularly known as “Kisan-Pran”.

questions.q: With reference to the National Planning Committee set up in 1938, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: It was constituted by Gandhi and chaired by Vallabhbhai Patel
options.B: It was constituted by Subhas Chandra Bose and chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru
options.C: It was constituted by Jawaharlal Nehru and chaired by M. Visvesvaraya
options.D: It was constituted by Rajendra Prasad and chaired by Subhas Chandra Bose

questions.explanation:
The National Planning Committee (NPC) was constituted in 1938 by Subhas Chandra Bose, who was then serving as the President of the Indian National Congress, having been elected to that position at the Haripura Session of 1938. Bose’s presidency was marked by a strong emphasis on industrialisation, economic planning, and modernisation as essential pillars of a future independent India. Acting on this vision, he set up the National Planning Committee and appointed Jawaharlal Nehru as its chairman. Nehru, who shared a deep intellectual commitment to planned economic development and had been significantly influenced by the Soviet model of centralised planning during his travels abroad, was a natural choice for the chairmanship.

The NPC brought together a remarkably diverse body of participants, including industrialists, scientists, economists, engineers, provincial government representatives, and Congress leaders, reflecting the broad, technocratic ambition of the exercise. It deliberated across numerous subcommittees on subjects ranging from agriculture, industries, and power to population, social services, and women’s roles in economic life. Though the NPC’s work was interrupted by the resignation of Congress ministries in 1939 and the political turbulence of the World War II years, it represented the first serious, systematic attempt at comprehensive economic planning for India and laid important intellectual groundwork for the planning apparatus that independent India would eventually build, culminating in the establishment of the Planning Commission in 1950, again under Nehru’s direction.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Mahatma Gandhi’s anti-untouchability campaign in the 1930s: 1. Harijan Sevak Sangh was established in 1932 to work for the upliftment of the so-called untouchables. 2. Gandhi launched the journal Harijan as part of this campaign. 3. Following this phase, Gandhi increasingly shifted emphasis from active political agitation toward constructive social work. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Harijan Sevak Sangh was established on 30 September 1932, following the signing of the Poona Pact between Gandhi and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. The Poona Pact was itself a direct outcome of Gandhi’s fast-unto-death in Yerawada Jail, undertaken in protest against the Communal Award of 1932, which had granted separate electorates to depressed classes. The Harijan Sevak Sangh was conceived as an institutional mechanism to carry out practical social reform work, including opening temples, wells, schools, and public spaces to the so-called untouchables, and was led by prominent Congress leaders, including Amritlal Thakkar (Thakkar Bapa) as its secretary.

Statement 2 is correct: Gandhi launched the weekly journal Harijan in February 1933 as the central publication vehicle for his anti-untouchability campaign. The journal replaced his earlier publications, Young India and Navajivan, in terms of focus, and served as a platform to educate uppercaste Hindu society about the moral and social necessity of eradicating untouchability. Gandhi also undertook an extensive Harijan Tour across India in 1933–34, travelling thousands of miles to spread awareness, collect funds for the Harijan Sevak Sangh, and directly engage communities on the issue.

Statement 3 is correct: Following the suspension of the Civil Disobedience Movement and through the mid-to-late 1930s, Gandhi consciously and deliberately shifted his primary emphasis from active political agitation against the British toward what he called constructive work, a comprehensive programme encompassing the eradication of untouchability, promotion of khadi and village industries, basic education through the Nai Talim (Basic Education) scheme, improvement of rural sanitation, upliftment of women, and HinduMuslim unity. Gandhi believed that inner social transformation and self-strengthening of Indian society were prerequisites for genuine political freedom, and this phase reflected his conviction that political swaraj without social swaraj would be hollow and incomplete.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Wardha Scheme of Basic Education: 1. It was based on the idea of imparting education through productive manual work. 2. The Zakir Hussain Committee was associated with its formulation. 3. It later came to be known as Nai Talim. 4. Its principal emphasis was on classical literary education. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The foundational philosophical principle of the Wardha Scheme was the idea of craft-centred, productive manual work as the medium of education. Gandhi proposed that all learning -- literacy, arithmetic, science, social studies, should be imparted not through conventional classroom instruction and rote memorisation, but through the activity of a productive craft such as spinning, weaving, carpentry, agriculture, or leatherwork. The child would learn academic subjects organically through engagement with the craft, making education simultaneously practical, economically productive, and intellectually stimulating. This approach was rooted in Gandhi’s broader conviction that the colonial education system had created a class of Indians alienated from manual labour, their own cultural roots, and the economic realities of village life.

Statement 2 is correct: Following Gandhi’s proposals at the All India National Education Conference held at Wardha in October 1937, a committee was constituted under the chairmanship of Dr. Zakir Hussain, the distinguished educationist who would later become the third President of India, to work out the detailed curriculum, methodology, and framework of the scheme. The Zakir Hussain Committee produced a comprehensive report that translated Gandhi’s broad philosophical vision into a concrete and implementable educational curriculum, specifying the craft-centred approach for children in the age group of 7 to 14 years across a seven-year basic education programme. The committee’s report became the foundational document of the scheme.

Statement 3 is correct: The Wardha Scheme of Basic Education came to be popularly known as Nai Talim, meaning “New Education” in Hindi and Urdu. Gandhi himself used this term extensively to describe the educational philosophy underlying the scheme. Nai Talim represented not merely a pedagogical method but a comprehensive social vision, of decentralised, self-sufficient village communities whose members were educated, skilled, and economically productive. Gandhi established the Hindustani Talimi Sangh in 1938 to propagate and implement Nai Talim, and it remained a central component of his constructive programme throughout the remaining years of his life.

Statement 4 is incorrect: Classical literary education was precisely what the Wardha Scheme sought to move away from. Gandhi was a sharp critic of the prevailing colonial education system, which privileged English-medium instruction, literary and clerical skills, and bookish academic learning divorced from practical life. He argued that this system produced graduates fit only for clerical employment under the colonial administration, while fostering contempt for manual labour and village life. The Wardha Scheme deliberately de-emphasised classical literary education and placed productive craft work at the centre, making Statement 4 directly contradictory to the scheme’s foundational purpose.

questions.q: With reference to Subhas Chandra Bose and the Tripuri Session of the Indian National Congress, consider the following statements: 1. Subhas Chandra Bose was re-elected Congress President at the Tripuri Session held in 1939 despite opposition from the right wing within the Congress. 2. Bose proposed that Congress should demand independence from the British within six months and prepare for a final struggle. 3. The Pant Proposal strengthened Bose’s freedom to appoint a Working Committee entirely of his choice. How many of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Subhas Chandra Bose was re-elected as Congress President at the Tripuri Session held in March 1939 at Tripuri, near Jabalpur (present-day Madhya Pradesh). He defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya, who was the candidate backed by Mahatma Gandhi and the right-wing Gandhian faction within the Congress. Gandhi took Sitaramayya’s defeat personally, remarking that it was more his defeat than Sitaramayya’s. Despite winning the election, Bose faced sustained opposition from the old guard and the conservative wing of the Congress throughout the session.

Statement 2 is correct: Bose advocated a more assertive and confrontational approach toward British rule. He proposed that Congress issue an ultimatum demanding complete independence within six months, and that in the event of noncompliance by the British, Congress should launch a mass civil disobedience movement, what he described as a “final struggle” for freedom. This position was fundamentally at odds with the more cautious approach favoured by Gandhi and the right wing, who believed the time was not yet ripe for such a decisive step.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The Pant Resolution, moved by Govind Ballabh Pant at the Tripuri Session, severely curtailed Bose’s authority rather than strengthening it. The resolution required the newly re-elected president to constitute the Working Committee in accordance with the wishes of Mahatma Gandhi, effectively stripping Bose of the freedom to appoint members of his own choosing. This resolution was a decisive blow to Bose’s authority and rendered his presidency largely ineffective. Unable to function independently and facing constant obstruction, Bose resigned from the Congress presidency in April 1939 and subsequently founded the Forward Bloc.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Eka Movement (1921–22): 1. The movement was led by Madari Pasi. 2. The peasants demanded a reduction in rent and the collection of revenue in cash instead of produce. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Eka Movement of 1921–22 was led by Madari Pasi and was centred mainly in Hardoi, Bahraich, Sitapur and Barabanki districts of Uttar Pradesh.

Statement 2 is correct: The peasants protested against excessive rent demands and insisted that rent should be collected in cash rather than in kind due to high inflation.

questions.q: Who was elected as the President of the Congress Socialist Party during its inception?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Acharya Narendra Dev was formally elected as the President of the Congress Socialist Party (CSP) during its foundational conference in Bombay in October 1934.

Jai Prakash Narayan served as the General Secretary.

Minoo Masani and Meherally were key foundational leaders but did not hold the presidential office.

Additional facts: • The formal foundation of the Congress Socialist Party took place in October 1934 in Bombay. • The conceptual origins of the party trace back to intense Marxist and socialist discussions among young Congressmen incarcerated in Nasik jail during the Civil Disobedience Movement. • The party operated as a cohesive ideological bloc strictly within the organisational framework of the Indian National Congress rather than forming a separate political entity. • The primary objective was to radicalise the mainstream Congress program and direct the national movement toward socialist structural reforms. • The socialists fundamentally rejected the growing parliamentary constitutionalism and council-entry programs favoured by the dominant Congress right-wing faction. • The party’s agrarian program demanded the complete abolition of the zamindari system without providing any financial compensation to the landlords. • A core economic demand included the total cancellation of oppressive debts owed by impoverished peasants and agricultural labourers. • The socialists actively advocated for the statutory recognition of both trade unions and kisan sabhas (peasant organisations) to integrate class struggles into the antiimperialist fight. • The party explicitly demanded the transfer of all sovereign political and economic power directly to the producing masses.

questions.q: Who successfully led the fierce peasant struggle to restore the Bakasht lands in the Barahiya Taal region?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Karyanand Sharma led the intense agrarian agitation against local zamindars for the restoration of Bakasht lands in the Barahiya Taal area of Munger district.

Yadunandan Sharma organised the parallel peasant movement in the Reora area of Gaya district.

Rahul Sankrityayan led the prominent agrarian Satyagraha in the Amwari region of Saran district.

Additional facts: • Bakasht lands were specific agricultural plots that zamindars had confiscated from tenant farmers who defaulted on rent during the Great Depression. • The Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha orchestrated this massive, organised campaign for land restoration between the years 1937 and 1939. • Zamindars frequently deployed armed retainers and thugs to violently suppress and assault peasant activists during these systemic protests. • Rahul Sankrityayan suffered severe physical injuries from zamindar thugs and was subsequently sentenced to six months in prison for his role in Amwari. • The immense grassroots pressure forced the newly elected Congress Ministry to pass the Bihar Tenancy (Amendment) Act. • The provincial government was also compelled to enact the specific Bakasht Land Disputes Settlement Act of 1938 to pacify the agrarian unrest. • Swami Sahajanand Saraswati originally founded the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1929 specifically to mobilise peasants against zamindari abuses. • Karyanand Sharma eventually emerged as a prominent leader within both the Communist Party of India and the All India Kisan Sabha.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the Forward Bloc is incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct

options.A: The foundational constitution explicitly restricted primary membership of the organisation strictly to existing Indian National Congress members.
options.B: The organisation’s first All-India Conference declared its primary political objective to be the establishment of a socialist state.
options.C: Sarat Chandra Bose was elected as the inaugural General Secretary of the party during its foundational phase.
options.D: Sardar Sardul Singh Caveeshar assumed the acting presidency of the party immediately following Subhas Chandra Bose’s arrest.

questions.explanation:
Lal Shankarlal was elected as the first General Secretary of the Forward Bloc, not Sarat Chandra Bose. While Sarat Chandra Bose (Subhas’s elder brother) was a political and financial pillar for the Left Consolidation, Kamath was the specific architect handling the organisational machinery as General Secretary.

Additional facts: • The Forward Bloc officially held its first AllIndia Conference in Nagpur between June 18 and June 22, 1940. • The Nagpur conference passed a definitive organisational resolution titled “All Power to the Indian People.” • The party’s Working Committee specifically organised a nationwide “National Struggle Week” from April 6 to April 13, 1940, to mobilise grassroots anti-war resistance. • Subhas Chandra Bose officially launched the party’s dedicated English weekly mouthpiece, identically titled Forward Bloc, in August 1939 to propagate socialist editorials. • Prominent regional organisers included Mukundilal Sircar and B. V. A. Annapurniah, who were tasked with building the party’s cadre base in Bengal and Andhra, respectively. • The Forward Bloc actively allied with the Muslim Students Federation to launch the militant Anti-Holwell Monument agitation in Calcutta during July 1940. • The British colonial administration formally declared the Forward Bloc an illegal, banned organisation in 1942 under the Defence of India Rules. • The party’s economic manifesto explicitly called for state ownership of large-scale industries while simultaneously supporting the tactical continuation of village industries for mass rural employment.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs related to the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935: 1. Sindh Created as a separate province 2. Burma Retained as part of the British India administration 3. Orissa Created as a new province How many of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correctly matched: Sindh was separated from the Bombay Presidency and constituted as a distinct province under the Government of India Act, 1935. Prior to this, Sindh had been administratively part of Bombay Presidency since 1847, and the demand for a separate Sindh province had been a longstanding aspiration of Muslim political leadership in the region, as Muslims constituted a majority of its population. The separation was also endorsed by the Simon Commission report of 1930 and featured prominently in the demands placed before the Round Table Conferences. Sindh thus became one of the newly created provinces that came into existence under the 1935 Act.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched: Burma was not retained as part of British India; rather, it was formally separated from British India under the Government of India Act, 1935, and given a separate constitution and administrative framework of its own through the Government of Burma Act, 1935, enacted simultaneously. Burma had been annexed progressively and administered as a province of British India since 1886. Its separation had been debated for years, with Burmese nationalists themselves divided on the issue, some fearing separation would deprive Burma of the benefits of Indian constitutional reforms. Nevertheless, the 1935 legislation formally severed Burma’s constitutional link with British India, and it became a separately administered Crown colony with effect from 1 April 1937.

Pair 3 is correctly matched: Orissa was carved out as a separate province under the Government of India Act, 1935, with effect from 1 April 1936. Previously, the Oriya-speaking regions had been amalgamated within the Bihar and Orissa provinces, which had itself been separated from Bengal in 1912. The movement for a distinct Oriya-speaking province, based on linguistic and cultural identity, had been sustained for decades, and the 1935 Act finally gave it constitutional recognition. Orissa thus became one of the new provinces created by the Act, alongside Sindh, and both came into formal existence on 1 April 1936 when provincial autonomy provisions were operationalised.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding peasant movements in colonial India: 1. The Uttar Pradesh Kisan Sabha was formed in February 1918. 2. Baba Ramchandra emerged as an important peasant leader in Oudh during the 1920s. 3. The Bardoli Satyagraha was led by Jawaharlal Nehru. 4. The Tebhaga Movement demanded that two-thirds of the produce should go to sharecroppers. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Uttar Pradesh Kisan Sabha was established in February 1918 through the efforts of leaders such as Indra Narayan Dwivedi, Gauri Shankar Mishra and Madan Mohan Malaviya.

Statement 2 is correct: Baba Ramchandra emerged as a prominent peasant leader in Oudh and played a major role in strengthening the peasant movement there. Statement 3 is incorrect: The Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928 was led by Vallabhbhai Patel, not Jawaharlal Nehru. After its success, Patel received the title “Sardar” from the women of Bardoli.

Statement 4 is correct: The Tebhaga Movement in Bengal demanded that sharecroppers should retain two-thirds of the produce while landlords should receive only one-third.

questions.q: Why did both the Congress and the Muslim League reject the August Offer?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Congress wanted Dominion Status, while the Muslim League wanted provincial autonomy
options.B: Congress opposed war participation, while the Muslim League opposed minority safeguards
options.C: Congress wanted federation, while the Muslim League wanted a stronger central government
options.D: Congress wanted complete independence, while the Muslim League wanted clear acceptance of the Pakistan demand

questions.explanation:
Congress rejected the August Offer primarily because it fell far short of its demand for complete independence. By 1940, Congress had long moved beyond accepting Dominion Status as a satisfactory objective. The offer’s promise of Dominion Status only after the war, combined with the limited expansion of the Executive Council under the continued overriding authority of the Viceroy, was seen as an inadequate and evasive response to India’s demand for full self-government. Congress also strongly objected to the minority veto provision, viewing it as a deliberate British mechanism to perpetuate communal divisions and obstruct meaningful constitutional progress.

The Muslim League rejected the offer because it contained no explicit recognition of the Pakistan demand that Jinnah had formally advanced at the Lahore Session in March 1940. Although the minority veto provision broadly served the League’s strategic interests, Jinnah sought a clear British acknowledgement of the League’s claim that Muslim majority regions should have the right to separate sovereign political arrangements. The absence of such recognition made the offer unacceptable to the League.

The simultaneous rejection by both organisations, though for entirely different reasons, illustrated the deepening political deadlock between Congress, the Muslim League, and the British colonial government, each operating from positions that had become increasingly irreconcilable and that would continue to shape the course of the independence struggle.

questions.q: Which of the following was not a feature of the constitutional proposals offered under the Cripps Mission (1942)?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct

options.A: Grant of Dominion Status to India immediately after the end of the war
options.B: Constitution-making by an elected Constituent Assembly after the war
options.C: Immediate transfer of full executive authority to Indian leaders during the war
options.D: Right of provinces to remain outside the proposed Indian Union

questions.explanation: The Cripps Mission refused to transfer full executive authority during the war. Churchill and the War Cabinet were firmly opposed to any dilution of executive control in wartime. When Congress pressed for real power at the centre as a condition for cooperation, Cripps could not concede this. Gandhi captured this limitation precisely with his dismissal of the proposals as a “post-dated cheque on a failing bank”, and it became the primary reason Congress rejected the Mission.

questions.q: The longest-lasting parallel government during the Quit India Movement was established at which of the following places?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Satara Prati Sarkar in Maharashtra was the longest-lasting parallel government of the Quit India Movement, functioning from 1943 to 1945. Led primarily by Nana Patil, it was also the most administratively developed, running its own courts (Nyayadan Mandals), revenue collection, village defence squads (Toofan Senas), and social reform programmes including suppression of the liquor trade.

Ballia under Chittu Pandey lasted only a few days in August 1942 before British forces reimposed control, the most short-lived of all parallel governments despite its dramatic impact.

Tamluk’s Jatiya Sarkar in Bengal, proclaimed in December 1942, was sustained and functional but shorter in duration than Satara.

questions.q: The Indian Independence League in East Asia was initially led by which of the following leaders?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Indian Independence League (IIL) in East Asia was initially led by Rash Behari Bose, the veteran revolutionary who had lived in exile in Japan since 1915 after escaping British pursuit following revolutionary activities in India. Over the decades, he developed strong political and social connections in Japan, which made him the most credible senior Indian nationalist figure in East Asia.

He presided over the Bangkok Conference of June 1942, where the IIL was formally organised as the political umbrella body for coordinating the Indian independence movement in Southeast Asia, alongside the military efforts that were taking shape through the Indian National Army under Mohan Singh.

Recognising that the movement required a leader with far greater mass appeal and contemporary political stature across India, Rash Behari Bose facilitated the transfer of leadership to Subhas Chandra Bose after his arrival in Southeast Asia in 1943. At the Singapore Conference in July 1943, Rash Behari Bose formally handed over leadership of the IIL to Subhas Chandra Bose. Thereafter, Subhas assumed command of the INA, revitalised the movement, and went on to establish the Provisional Government of Azad Hind in October 1943.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Vallabhbhai Patel came to be popularly known as “Sardar” after the Bardoli Satyagraha. Reason (R): The women of Bardoli honoured Patel with the title after the successful peasant movement of 1928. Select the correct answer:
questions.question_type: Assertion and Reason — Standard Relationship Evaluation

options.A: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.B: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.explanation:
Assertion (A) is true: Vallabhbhai Patel became widely known as “Sardar” after the success of the Bardoli Satyagraha in 1928.

Reason (R) is true: The women of Bardoli conferred the title “Sardar” upon Patel in recognition of his leadership during the peasant struggle. Therefore, R correctly explains A.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the Provisional Government of Azad Hind is correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: It was established in Berlin in 1941 under the leadership of Subhas Chandra Bose
options.B: It was formed in Singapore in 1943 under the leadership of Subhas Chandra Bose
options.C: It received diplomatic recognition from the Allied powers during the Second World War
options.D: It was headed by Rash Behari Bose as its chief executive

questions.explanation:
The Provisional Government of Azad Hind (Free India) was formally proclaimed on 21 October 1943 in Singapore by Subhas Chandra Bose, who assumed the roles of Head of State, Prime Minister, and Minister for War and Foreign Affairs. Revered as “Netaji,” Bose sought to present Azad Hind as the legitimate sovereign government of an independent India in exile.

The government established the institutional framework of a functioning state, including a cabinet, judicial arrangements, civil administrative structure, and its own currency framework, while exercising authority through the Indian National Army (INA) as its armed wing.

Azad Hind received diplomatic recognition from several Axis-aligned states, including Germany, Japan, Italy, Croatia, Burma, the Philippines, and Manchukuo, lending it international symbolic legitimacy within the wartime geopolitical context. Its creation marked the most serious attempt by Indian nationalists to establish an alternative sovereign authority outside British control through armed struggle.

questions.q: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands were renamed by the Azad Hind Government as which of the following?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: When Japan transferred administrative control of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to the Provisional Government of Azad Hind in November 1943, Subhas Chandra Bose renamed them “Shaheed Dweep” (Martyr Islands) and “Swaraj Dweep” (Selfrule Islands) respectively. Bose personally visited the islands in December 1943 and hoisted the flag of Azad Hind, a moment of immense symbolic significance as it represented the Azad Hind Government exercising actual territorial sovereignty over Indian soil, however limited in extent.

questions.q: Why did Junagadh emerge as a contentious issue during the integration of princely states?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Its Hindu ruler sought accession to Pakistan as the state had a Muslim-majority population
options.B: Its Muslim ruler sought accession to Pakistan despite the state having a Hindu-majority population
options.C: The British government retained direct administrative control over the state after independence
options.D: The state became the subject of simultaneous territorial claims by both Nepal and India

questions.explanation:
Junagadh presented a unique and provocative challenge to the integration process. The Nawab of Junagadh, Mahabat Khan, acceded to Pakistan in August 1947 despite the state being geographically located in the Kathiawar peninsula of western India, sharing no territorial contiguity with Pakistan, and having an overwhelmingly Hindu-majority population of approximately 80%.

Pakistan’s acceptance of this accession was constitutionally significant and politically problematic from India’s perspective, as it directly contradicted the principle the Muslim League had invoked to justify Pakistan’s creation, namely, that Muslim-majority areas should form Pakistan. If the personal decision of a Muslim ruler could determine accession irrespective of geography and demographic composition, it would weaken India’s position regarding other princely states, particularly Hyderabad and Kashmir.

India refused to recognise the accession, imposed economic pressure, and supported political opposition within the state. The Nawab eventually fled to Pakistan, after which Indian forces entered Junagadh. A plebiscite held in February 1948 overwhelmingly favoured accession to India, bringing the issue to a formal conclusion in India’s favour.

questions.q: Arrange the following events relating to the accession of Jammu and Kashmir in chronological order: 1. Mountbatten’s visit to Hari Singh 2. Tribal invasion backed by Pakistan 3. Signing of the Instrument of Accession Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.question_type: Chronological Order — Correct Sequence
questions.explanation:
Mountbatten’s visit to Hari Singh occurred in June 1947, before independence, when Mountbatten travelled to Srinagar to personally persuade Hari Singh to decide on accession before the transfer of power. Hari Singh avoided a direct meeting, feigning illness, and refused to commit to either dominion.

The tribal invasion backed by Pakistan began on 22 October 1947, when Pakistani-backed Pashtun lashkars crossed into Kashmir and advanced rapidly toward Srinagar, forcing Hari Singh’s hand.

The Instrument of Accession was signed on 26 October 1947, after Hari Singh’s desperate appeal to India and V. P. Menon’s rushed visit to Srinagar to secure the formal accession document, enabling Indian troops to be airlifted the following day.

questions.question_type: Match the Following — Two-List Matching — Answer-Code Matrix
questions.explanation:
Baba Ramchandra emerged as an important peasant leader in the Oudh peasant movement.

Vallabhbhai Patel led the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928 against enhanced land revenue demands.

Swami Sahajanand Saraswati founded the Bihar Kisan Sabha to fight for peasant rights and the abolition of zamindari.

Madari Pasi led the Eka Movement of 1921–22 in parts of Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: Where was Mahatma Gandhi on 15 August 1947?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.D: In Calcutta working for communal peace

questions.explanation: While the rest of the country was celebrating independence and Jawaharlal Nehru was delivering his “Tryst with Destiny” speech in New Delhi on August 15, 1947, Mahatma Gandhi chose not to participate in the festivities. He was stationed in a dilapidated house in Beliaghata, Calcutta, fasting and holding prayer meetings to quell the severe communal riots that had erupted between Hindus and Muslims in the wake of Partition.

questions.q: Who prominently co-founded the Utkal Provincial Kisan Sabha to mobilise peasants across the coastal districts?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Malati Choudhury was a central architect of the Utkal Provincial Kisan Sabha, tirelessly organising massive peasant awakenings against severe zamindari exploitation across the Odisha region.

Additional facts: • The Utkal Provincial Kisan Sabha was formally established in 1935 to systematically combat the oppressive land revenue structures prevalent throughout coastal Odisha. • Co-founders: Malati Choudhury, Gopabandhu Choudhury, and Nabakrushna Choudhury collaborated to build a robust socialist and agrarian political foundation within the province. • Leadership: H. K. Mahatab was elected as the President, and Malati Choudhury as the Secretary of the Utkal Kisan Sangha • First Conference: The first Utkal Kisan Conference was held at Cuttack Town Hall on 10 June 1935, under the Presidentship of Mohanlal Gautam of Uttar Pradesh. • Orissa Tenancy Act Amendment: The Sabha fiercely demanded immediate legislative amendment of the restrictive Orissa Tenancy Act to secure permanent, legal occupancy rights for actual cultivators. • Abolition of Begar: The movement explicitly campaigned for the complete abolition of illegal feudal levies and forced labour (begar) exacted by landlords from the peasantry. • Praja Mandal Collaboration: The regional peasant awakening deeply intersected with parallel Praja Mandal agitations demanding democratic rights within neighbouring Odia princely states. • Vernacular Literature: Organisers actively printed and distributed radical agrarian literature translated into the vernacular Odia language to raise grassroots political consciousness. • Political Context: The destiny of Odisha’s peasants was guided by Congress Socialists, who played a central role in the Kisan movement. • Mass Mobilisation: Activists organised massive, disciplined peasant marches and public rallies to physically demonstrate severe agrarian discontent against entrenched local zamindars. • Rent Reduction Demand: The movement demanded immediate reduction of land revenue and rent to alleviate peasant distress.

questions.q: Which armed 1946 working-class insurrection was brutally suppressed by the princely state administration of Travancore?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Punnapra-Vayalar Uprising was a specific armed communist rebellion directed against the autocratic administration of the Travancore princely state.

Karivellur, Kayyur, and Morazha struggles were all prominent communist-led agrarian uprisings located strictly within the directly Britishadministered Malabar district.

Additional facts: • The formal general strike that precipitated the most violent confrontations was officially launched on October 22, 1946. • The uprising was directed against the oppressive rule of C. P. Ramaswami Iyer, the Diwan of Travancore • The revolt is named after the two places in Alappuzha district where it took place: beginning in Punnapra and ending in Vayalar. • Kayyur Incident (1941): The Kayyur agitation famously culminated in the execution of four young communist peasants by the British colonial judiciary. 3 Karivellur and Kavumbayi Struggles: These concurrent struggles in neighbouring Malabar specifically focused on violently preventing powerful landlords from exporting hoarded paddy during the famine period. • The revolt weakened the authority of the Diwan. • The Maharajah agreed to accede the kingdom to the Indian Union a week after the assassination attempt. • Pattom Thanu Pillai became the first Chief Minister of Travancore-Cochin (1948) after Travancore’s integration.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Nagpur Conference of the Forward Bloc (1940): 1. It declared the Forward Bloc as a socialist party. 2. It adopted the slogan “All Power to the Indian People.” Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Nagpur Conference of the All India Forward Bloc, held in 1940, was a landmark organisational milestone in which the Forward Bloc formally declared itself a socialist party. It adopted a clearly left-wing ideological orientation, positioning itself as a radical alternative to what Bose and his supporters perceived as the overly moderate and compromising tendencies within the mainstream Indian National Congress. This declaration gave the Forward Bloc a distinct ideological identity, differentiating it both from the Gandhian Congress right and from other existing socialist formations within the broader nationalist movement.

Statement 2 is correct: The Nagpur Conference adopted the powerful slogan “All Power to the Indian People”, which encapsulated the Forward Bloc’s core ideological demand, the complete transfer of political, economic, and social authority from British colonial hands to the Indian people themselves. This slogan reflected the party’s rejection of dominion status or any partial transfer of power and its insistence on full, unconditional independence accompanied by a fundamental restructuring of political power in favour of the masses, particularly workers and peasants.

questions.q: Who among the following British officials ordered firing on the unarmed crowd at Jallianwala Bagh in 1919?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Option C is correct: Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to open fire on the unarmed gathering at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, on 13 April 1919 without any warning. The massacre became one of the most tragic incidents of British rule in India.

Option A is incorrect: Michael O’Dwyer was the Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab at the time of the massacre. He supported Dyer’s actions and the repressive measures taken in Punjab, but he did not personally order the firing at Jallianwala Bagh. Later, Udham Singh assassinated Michael O’Dwyer in 1940 in revenge for the massacre.

Option B is incorrect: Lord Chelmsford was the Viceroy of India from 1916 to 1921. Although he was the head of the British administration in India during the incident, he was not the officer who directly ordered the firing.

Option D is incorrect: Sir Sidney Rowlatt was the British judge who headed the Rowlatt Commission. The commission’s recommendations led to the passage of the repressive Rowlatt Act (1919), but he had no direct role in the Jallianwala Bagh firing.

questions.q: According to historian A.J.P Taylor, which of the following events became the “decisive moment when Indians were alienated from British rule”?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Historian A. J. P Taylor described the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919 as the “decisive moment when Indians were alienated from British rule.”

The massacre occurred on 13 April 1919 at Amritsar when Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire on an unarmed gathering without warning.

The incident deeply shocked Indian public opinion and destroyed the faith of many Indians in the fairness of British rule.

The tragedy became a turning point in the Indian national movement and strengthened the demand for complete independence from British rule.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Hunter Committee: 1. The Hunter Committee was formed to investigate the disturbances in Punjab following the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. 2. The committee was constituted on the orders of Edwin Montagu, the Secretary of State for India. 3. Sir Sidney Rowlatt headed the committee. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Disorders Inquiry Committee, popularly known as the Hunter Committee or Hunter Commission, was constituted to investigate the disturbances in Punjab, Bombay and Delhi, including the events related to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

Statement 2 is correct: The committee was formed on the orders of Edwin Montagu, the Secretary of State for India, after widespread criticism of British actions in Punjab.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The committee was headed by Lord William Hunter, not Sir Sidney Rowlatt. Sidney Rowlatt had earlier chaired the Rowlatt Commission, whose recommendations led to the Rowlatt Act of 1919.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding provincial autonomy under the Government of India Act, 1935: 1. Dyarchy in provinces was abolished. 2. Bicameral legislatures were introduced in all British Indian provinces. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Government of India Act, 1935, abolished dyarchy at the provincial level, which had originally been introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919, under the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms. Under the 1919 framework, provincial subjects were bifurcated into “reserved” subjects, administered by the Governor and his executive council without legislative accountability and “transferred” subjects, administered by ministers responsible to the elected legislature. This division created an awkward and often dysfunctional dual system of governance at the provincial level. The 1935 Act swept away this division entirely and introduced full responsible government in the provinces, wherein all provincial subjects were placed under ministers collectively responsible to the elected provincial legislature. Governors retained certain special powers and discretionary functions, but the substantive governance of provinces was made accountable to elected representatives. Notably, while dyarchy was abolished in the provinces, the 1935 Act paradoxically introduced dyarchy at the Centre, though, as discussed separately, this central federal scheme never came into operation.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Bicameral legislatures, consisting of a Legislative Assembly (lower house) and a Legislative Council (upper house), were not introduced in all eleven British Indian provinces. The 1935 Act established bicameral legislatures only in six provinces: Madras, Bombay, Bengal, the United Provinces, Bihar, and Assam. The remaining five provinces, Punjab, the NorthWest Frontier Province (NWFP), the Central Provinces, Orissa, and Sind, retained unicameral legislatures consisting of a single Legislative Assembly. The decision to establish bicameral or unicameral structures was calibrated according to the administrative size, population, and political complexity of each province, making it incorrect to generalise that all provinces received bicameral legislatures under the Act.

questions.q: Which of the following personalities is not associated with the observance of the ‘Day of Deliverance’ in December 1939:
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Mahatma Gandhi was not associated with the observance of the Day of Deliverance. On the contrary, the Day of Deliverance was fundamentally directed against the Congress and its provincial ministries, the very political organisation Gandhi led and whose record of governance he had championed. Gandhi defended the Congress ministries’ performance in office and rejected the characterisation that they had suppressed or discriminated against minorities and marginalised communities. His association with this observance would have been entirely self-contradictory.

The Day of Deliverance was observed on 22 December 1939, called by Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the All India Muslim League to celebrate what they described as liberation from the alleged tyranny and Hindu domination of Congress provincial ministries following their resignation in October and November 1939. The occasion brought together a politically diverse coalition united primarily by their opposition to or disillusionment with Congress’s governance.

Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the principal architect of the Day of Deliverance, using it as a powerful political instrument to consolidate Muslim opinion against Congress and to advance the League’s claim that it, not Congress, was the sole legitimate representative of Indian Muslims. B. R. Ambedkar participated and expressed solidarity with the observance, consistent with his longstanding criticism of Congress for what he perceived as its failure to genuinely address Dalit rights and its tendency to subsume Dalit political interests within a broader nationalist framework that remained dominated by upper caste leadership. E. V. Ramasamy Periyar, the radical social reformer and founder of the Self-Respect Movement in South India, also associated himself with the occasion, reflecting his deep hostility toward Congress, which he viewed as an instrument of Brahminical and upper caste dominance over the non Brahmin and Dravidian populations of the south.

questions.q: During whose Viceroyalty was the Rowlatt Act passed in India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Rowlatt Act was passed in March 1919 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921). • The Act was officially known as the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act and was based on the recommendations of the Rowlatt Commission headed by Sir Sidney Rowlatt. • It empowered the British government to detain individuals without trial, impose restrictions on freedom of speech and assembly, and conduct secret trials. 3 The Act was widely opposed across India and led to the launch of the Rowlatt Satyagraha under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi.

Option A is incorrect: Lord Curzon served as Viceroy from 1899 to 1905 and is mainly associated with the Partition of Bengal in 1905.

Option C is incorrect: Lord Irwin served as Viceroy from 1926 to 1931 and is associated with the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and the Civil Disobedience Movement.

Option D is incorrect: Lord Wavell served as Viceroy from 1943 to 1947 and is known for the Wavell Plan and the Simla Conference of 1945.

questions.q: Which of the following factors contributed to the rise of anti-British sentiments in India after the First World War? 1. Rise in prices and taxation 2. Jallianwala Bagh massacre 3. Introduction of dyarchy under the MontaguChelmsford Reforms 4. Abolition of Permanent Settlement Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
After the First World War, Indians expected constitutional concessions from the British government in return for India’s support during the war. However, instead of reforms satisfying Indian aspirations, several developments generated widespread resentment.

Economic hardship increased due to inflation, rising taxation, unemployment and a decline in industrial production.

The brutal suppression in Punjab, particularly the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, exposed the repressive nature of colonial rule.

The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms introduced dyarchy, but Indians found it inadequate and deceptive because real powers remained with the British.

Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 and was unrelated to post-war developments. Hence, statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Tripuri Session crisis (1939): 1. Subhas Chandra Bose defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya in the Congress presidential election. 2. Gandhi remarked that Pattabhi’s defeat was his own defeat. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: At the Tripuri Session of 1939, held near Jabalpur in present-day Madhya Pradesh, Subhas Chandra Bose defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya in the Congress presidential election. Sitaramayya was the candidate backed by Mahatma Gandhi and the Gandhian right wing of the Congress. Bose, who sought re-election on a platform of uncompromising anti-imperialism and a more confrontational approach toward the British, secured a clear majority despite sustained opposition from the old guard. The margin of victory, while not overwhelming, was politically decisive and represented a significant, if short-lived, assertion of the radical left against the dominant Gandhian faction.

Statement 2 is correct: Gandhi responded to Sitaramayya’s defeat with politically charged remark that Pattabhi’s defeat was more his own defeat than Pattabhi’s. This statement was deeply significant, as it transformed what had been an organisational election into a direct referendum on Gandhi’s authority within the Congress, and effectively signalled to the broader Congress membership where their loyalties were expected to lie. The remark galvanised the Gandhian majority within the Congress Working Committee, most of whose members declined to serve under Bose, precipitating the crisis that ultimately led to the Pant Resolution, Bose’s effective marginalisation, his resignation from the presidency in April 1939, and his subsequent founding of the Forward Bloc.

questions.q: The “secession clause” in the Cripps Proposals is considered significant primarily because it:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Provided a constitutional basis for provinces to remain outside the proposed Union, thereby strengthening the possibility of future partition
options.B: Ended the autonomy of the princely states within the proposed constitutional framework
options.C: Guaranteed immediate independence to India upon acceptance of the proposals
options.D: Abolished the system of separate electorates in the future constitutional arrange

questions.explanation:
The secession clause in the Cripps Proposals stipulated that provinces unwilling to join the proposed post-war Indian Union could choose not to participate in the new constitutional framework and instead negotiate separate arrangements with Britain. Its primary significance lay in providing, for the first time, an explicit constitutional opening for the territorial disintegration of India, by acknowledging that not all parts of British India were required to remain within a single future union.

Congress strongly opposed this provision because it appeared to grant constitutional legitimacy to the logic underlying the Muslim League’s Pakistan demand after the Lahore Resolution of 1940. By recognising provincial non-participation as a formal constitutional option rather than merely a political claim, the clause substantially strengthened the League’s negotiating leverage and made the prospect of partition constitutionally conceivable. This marked a major shift in the constitutional discourse surrounding India’s future.

questions.q: Operation Zero Hour refers to which of the following actions taken by the British during the Quit India Movement?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: The launch of underground Congress Radio broadcasts to sustain the movement
options.B: The pre-dawn arrest of top Congress leaders on 9 August 1942 to suppress the movement at its outset
options.C: The military offensive launched by the Indian National Army in the Imphal region
options.D: The British strategy for evacuation in response to the Japanese advance in Southeast Asia

questions.explanation:
Operation Zero Hour was the codename for the British government’s pre-emptive crackdown carried out in the early hours of 9 August 1942, just hours after the All India Congress Committee passed the Quit India Resolution at Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay, on the night of 8 August. In a swift and coordinated operation, Gandhi, the entire Congress Working Committee, and virtually all major Congress leaders across the country were arrested simultaneously before they could organise or direct the movement. Gandhi was detained at the Aga Khan Palace, Pune, where he remained imprisoned until 1944.

The British strategy was clear: by removing the entire national leadership at the very outset, they intended to prevent the emergence of a centrally coordinated mass uprising. However, the strategy achieved only limited success. Instead of suppressing resistance entirely, the arrests triggered a spontaneous and leaderless rebellion across several parts of India, especially Bihar, eastern United Provinces, Maharashtra, and Bengal. Protesters attacked railway lines, telegraph offices, police stations, and other symbols of colonial authority, while in some regions parallel governments emerged, most notably at Satara in Maharashtra and Tamluk in Bengal.

questions.q: Arrange the following phases of the Quit India Movement in the correct chronological order: 1. Urban strikes and demonstrations 2. Rural rebellion and attacks on communication lines 3. Underground resistance and establishment of parallel governments Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.question_type: Chronological Order — Correct Sequence
questions.explanation:
The Quit India Movement (August 1942 onwards) unfolded in three broad, overlapping phases following the mass arrest of Congress leadership under Operation Zero Hour.

Urban strikes and demonstrations came first, erupting immediately after the arrests of 9 August 1942. Students, workers, and urban populations responded with hartals, processions, and strikes across major cities including Bombay, Ahmedabad, and Calcutta. This phase was spontaneous and emotionally charged, driven largely by outrage at the wholesale arrest of the national leadership.

Rural rebellion and attacks on communication lines followed as the movement spread beyond cities into the countryside, particularly in Bihar, eastern United Provinces, Bengal, and Maharashtra. Peasants and rural populations attacked police stations, cut telegraph wires, uprooted railway lines, and targeted other symbols of British administrative authority. This phase was significantly more intense and difficult to suppress than the urban agitation, and the British response included aerial strafing of villages in some areas.

Underground resistance and parallel governments represented the final and most organised phase, emerging as overt agitation was suppressed by British force. Underground networks sustained the movement through pamphlets, courier systems, and the famous Congress Radio operated by Usha Mehta. In certain areas, notably Satara in Maharashtra under Nana Patil and Tamluk (Tamralipta) in Bengal, genuine parallel administrations were established that functioned independently of British authority for extended periods, representing the movement’s most radical political expression.

questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.C: Demanded the immediate transfer of political power exclusively to the Muslim League
options.A: Rejected the demand for partition and reaffirmed the idea of a united India
options.B: Accepted, in principle, the possibility of Pakistan through a plebiscite in Muslimmajority areas
options.D: Proposed a confederation of princely states as the basis of India’s future political structure

questions.explanation:
The C. Rajagopalachari Formula (CR Formula) of 1944 was historically significant because it marked the first serious attempt by a senior Congress leader to acknowledge, albeit conditionally, the possibility of partition as a negotiable political outcome rather than rejecting it outright. Rajagopalachari proposed it as a pragmatic effort to break the deadlock between the Congress and the Muslim League and to secure League cooperation in the struggle for independence.

Its principal provisions were that the Muslim League would support the Congress demand for immediate independence and cooperate in the formation of an interim government. After the war, a commission would demarcate contiguous districts in the northwest and northeast where Muslims formed an absolute majority, following which a plebiscite of all residents in those areas would determine whether they wished to form a separate sovereign state. If partition were approved, agreements would be negotiated regarding defence, commerce, and communications. Importantly, separation was to occur only after independence, not before.

Jinnah rejected the proposal, describing it as a “mutilated and moth-eaten Pakistan.” His objections included the fact that the plebiscite would involve all residents rather than only Muslims, that partition would be considered only after independence, and that continued common arrangements would dilute full sovereignty.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Khilafat issue helped in strengthening Hindu-Muslim unity during the national movement. Reason (R): Congress leaders fully supported the British policy towards Turkey.
questions.question_type: Assertion and Reason — Standard Relationship Evaluation

options.A: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
options.B: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

questions.explanation:
The Khilafat issue became an important basis for Hindu-Muslim unity because the Indian National Congress supported Muslim concerns regarding the position of the Khalifa of Turkey. Leaders like Mahatma Gandhi saw this as an opportunity to unite Indians against British imperialism. However, the reason statement is incorrect because Congress leaders opposed British policy towards Turkey. They criticised Britain for dismembering Turkey and removing the authority of the Khalifa after the First World War.

Thus, the assertion is true, but Reason is false.

questions.q: Why did the Gandhi-Jinnah Talks of 1944 fail?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Gandhi refused to consider any discussion on the question of Pakistan
